Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 8, verse 1 (part 1 of 3):

(The remainder of the introduction to the surah)

Those who seek the moral justification of the Islamic doctrine of jihad only in the causes and reasons for protecting Dar al-Islam (the abode of Islam) have, in fact, failed to assess the true worth and value of the Islamic system. They regard this system as something of lower rank than even a homeland, whereas from the Islamic point of view this notion is not correct. This is an entirely different idea, and it is what has come to dominate the Islamic conception. The reality is that Islam gives importance first to belief ('aqidah), then to the system that is founded upon that belief, and then to the society in which that system is established. These are the things that carry importance in the Islamic conception of life... As for land alone, in itself Islam attaches no importance to it. A land of Islam gains its importance only because in it the sovereignty of Allah Most High is established, and because it becomes a nursery of Islamic belief and, as a field for the Islamic system of life, it takes on the status of Dar al-Islam, and becomes a centre for the "movement of human liberation".

The protection of Dar al-Islam is also undertaken so that this belief, this system of life, and this society established in Dar al-Islam may be protected. Dar al-Islam in itself is not an independent goal, nor is the movement of Islamic jihad aimed solely at the protection of Dar al-Islam. Its protection is undertaken only so that the rule of God may be established there, and so that it may then be made a centre from which to spread over the entire surface of the earth and to convey the call of Islam to the whole of humankind. Thus, as it were, all of humanity is the subject of this religion, and the entire globe is its field of action.

As we have said earlier, whenever the work of spreading the religion begins, material obstacles are placed in its path by the political power of the time, the prevailing collective system of the time, and the customs and habits of the societies of the time. Then Islam, by its own strength, removes all these things from its path, so that it can address people directly, speak to their conscience and their thoughts, and so that there remains no material barrier between the preaching of the religion and the human being. After that, people are given the choice whether to accept the Islamic belief or not.

We should not be overawed by anyone regarding the Islamic doctrine of jihad, nor should we be influenced by the whisperings of the Orientalists. It is not appropriate, under pressure from present international circumstances, to give a modern interpretation of the Islamic doctrine of jihad. Doing so would destroy its spirit. The reality is that the circumstances and events which were related to a temporary defence would, even if they had not existed, still have led the Muslims to wage jihad in the same way as they did in the presence of those circumstances.

Direct study

We should only undertake a historical review of the Islamic system of life and see what matters it gives priority to, what its temperament is, and what it proclaims. What is its method? In making any definitive decisions about all these matters, we must distinguish between temporary and defensive measures and the permanent objective.

It is entirely correct that this religion also defends against aggressors, because jihiliyyah (ignorance) can under no circumstances tolerate it. The mere proclamation that there is no god but Allah is a great challenge to jihiliyyah, as is the declaration that no human being is the slave of another. It is not merely a verbal declaration; alongside it, a practical movement under a leadership is organised, and a distinct and entirely new society is founded which, politically, rejects all sovereignties other than that of Allah. All these things have always been intolerable to jihiliyyah. In short, the very existence of the Islamic system of life, in the historical form in which the Messenger (ﷺ) presented it, was sufficient for all the jahili societies of that time to rise up against it, since their very foundation rested on the principle that human beings should serve other human beings. They would strive to eliminate this religion and to defend their own existence. In these circumstances it was also necessary for the Islamic system of life to defend itself and to adopt measures of protection in dangerous conditions. This was an unavoidable necessity: together with the existence of Islam, its defence was also essential. It never happens that a newly emerging power immediately acquires an offensive position. There is a period in which one must defend oneself, but this cannot mean that Islam should continue defending itself forever. Indeed, it is also a reality that the very existence of Islam requires that, under suitable circumstances, it advance and deliver the whole of humanity from servitude to other than Allah. In this matter Islam does not accept any geographical limitation; it is contrary to the temperament of Islam to leave all of humanity wandering in the darkness of ignorance and error, suffering oppression, and to be content with reforming only one race or one particular people.

Sometimes it may also happen, in certain circumstances, that the systems supporting jahiliyyah adopt a soft attitude towards Islam. 

Sometimes circumstances may also arise in which the systems supporting jahiliyyah adopt a soft attitude towards Islam, do not attack it, and Islam likewise leaves them free within their geographical boundaries so that they may enslave people and rule over them; there is no interference and the Islamic movement is not extended to those limits. But this pause is temporary. The real policy is that Islam does not make peace with those jahili societies until they bow before the sovereignty of Islam and, by paying jizyah, provide proof that the doors of their country are open to the Islamic movement and that the government established within their borders is not an obstacle in the path of Islam. This is the temperament of this religion and its true purpose and objective, namely to free all of humanity from servitude to other than Allah and to bring it into the servitude of Allah alone.

There is the difference of heaven and earth between this conception of the religion of Islam and that conception which confines it within a limited territory. If we adopt this limited conception of Islam, then it becomes necessary for us to seek justifications for the expansion of Islam in the first century.

But if our conception of the Islamic system of life is that Islam is the system of life prescribed by Allah for all human beings, and that it is not related to any particular group or race of people, then the real reasons for Islam's expansionist character automatically become apparent to us. As long as this reality remains hidden from our minds, we wander seeking external causes for that expansion, whereas the true nature of the matter is only this: that the objective of Islam is the freedom of the whole of humanity and servitude to Allah, and whoever has this truth settled in his mind will feel no need to seek any other moral justification.

Two viewpoints

Regarding the Islamic doctrine of jihad, two viewpoints exist. One is that Islam was compelled to plunge into the battle of jihad because the jahili societies rose up to wipe it out. The other view is that Islam itself takes the initiative and enters the battle of jihad. Although in the early period it appears difficult to distinguish between these two conceptions, since in both cases Islam had to plunge into the battle of jihad, later on the difference becomes clear, and this brings about a great change in the outlook and consciousness of Muslims regarding Islam, and has far-reaching consequences.

According to the second viewpoint, Islam becomes a system of life that has been prescribed by Allah Himself. He wishes the whole of humanity to enter into the worship of Allah, that human beings be subject only to the command of Allah, that His Shari'ah be the law of the land, and that only Allah deserve divinity. When this viewpoint regarding Islam is adopted, it becomes its natural right to remove all obstacles that stand in its way, so that it can directly appeal to people's reason, consciousness and intuition. There is a great difference between this comprehensive conception of Islam and the conception according to which it is presented as a "regional and local" concept. If we regard it as a regional system, then its only right will be to defend its existence and survival within its regional boundaries. Both these conceptions of Islam influence the doctrine of jihad. Although apparently there seems to be no particular difference between them, in both cases the Muslims must plunge into the battle of jihad; yet as a result of these two conceptions the nature and reality of the doctrine of jihad changes.

Since Islam is not the religion of one nation or race, it has the natural right to be dynamic, because it is a divine system and is meant for the entire world. Therefore it is not necessary for it merely to wait, and then to advance and eliminate the false systems of life, tear away the veils of wrong customs and practices, and remove the fetters that have deprived the common people of the freedom of choosing and rejecting. In this matter Islam has only exercised the caution that it does not coerce any single individual. Rather, it attacks the collective order of life and the collective customs and habits, so that individuals may be protected from the wrong influences upon life that corrupt human nature and rob it of its freedom.

Islam has the right to take people out of servitude to other than Allah and bring them into the servitude of Allah alone, and to make its aim a reality: that there is no Lord and master besides Allah. All people are now free from the servitude of false masters. This can only happen when the Islamic system of life is established in this world, because it is only this system in which Allah Most High alone legislates for all human beings, whether they are rulers or ruled, white or black, far or near, poor or rich. In short, there is one kind of legislation before which all bow their heads. In all other systems apart from Islam, some human beings serve other human beings, because humans make laws for them; and legislation is in essence a major attribute of divinity. Whoever claims the right to legislate for human beings is, in fact, claiming lordship, whether or not he declares this claim in explicit words; and whoever accepts the claim of such a person has, in fact, taken him as his god, whether or not he declares it.

Keep well in mind that Islam is not merely a philosophy and theory, content with sermons and oratory and with presenting its concepts to people's ears; rather, it is a collective system of life which, advancing with great power and force, wishes to free people from servitude to other than Allah. The other collective systems are not competent to organise the collective life of human beings along the lines that Islam desires. Therefore Islam considers itself justified in uprooting these false systems from their foundations, so that they cannot become obstacles in the path of human freedom of thought. This is the meaning of "and the religion becomes entirely for Allah" (wa yakuna al-din kulluhu lillah), that is, in the Islamic system the original authority of legislation and sovereignty belongs to Allah Most High alone.

Some writers of the present age have not grasped this distinctive feature of the Islamic system of life, and they describe the Islamic doctrine of jihad as merely a defensive doctrine. These people have been overawed by the propaganda of the Orientalists that Islam spreads by the force of the sword and compels people to become Muslims. The Orientalists, in their own right, are well acquainted with the reality of the Islamic system, but their aim is to create misunderstandings about the reality of the Islamic doctrine of jihad. In the face of this situation, these writers arise and answer these questions, and for them there is no alternative but to seek the causes and reasons of a defensive war. These gentlemen entirely disregard the temperament of Islam and its objective, whereas according to the Islamic conception of life, it is Islam's duty to take the initiative and not merely to defend. The Western concept of religion has so firmly taken root in the minds of these defeated writers that they regard the Islamic system of life also as a religious belief having no concern with the practical and collective order of life. Therefore, in their view, the meaning of "Holy War" (jihad) is reduced to waging jihad in order to bring people into the religion and to impose a particular belief upon them, whereas the actual situation is entirely the opposite. Islam is a complete system of life for the whole of existence, and its foundation is the belief that this universe has a Creator who is also its sovereign and ruler, and who has prescribed this complete system for the whole of humanity. Accordingly, jihad means implementing this system upon human beings. As for whether someone adopts Islamic belief or not, that depends entirely on his free power of discernment. However, it is necessary that he have a free atmosphere in which to reflect freely, and for such an atmosphere to be available, the implementation of the Islamic system of life is essential. This is the true Islamic concept of religion, which is entirely different from the Western concept of religion.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verse 1 (part 2 of 3):

After the emergence of the Islamic society and the establishment of the Islamic system of life within it, Allah grants this society the authority to advance, to take control of power, and to enforce this system across the whole earth as far as possible. As for whether an individual accepts this system of life consciously or not, everyone is free in this matter. Depending on circumstances and opportunities, it has sometimes happened that Allah restrained the Muslims from armed jihad. This was not a permanent policy but the demand of temporary circumstances and considerations. It was done on account of the practical requirements of the movement. We have, in this discussion, examined verses of different periods and specified their meanings. In light of this, we should distinguish between the policies that were settled on various occasions and the principle and objective that has been settled for all time, and we should not neglect the permanent commands in view of the temporary ones.

Now the only point left before us is: what is the nature of the Islamic doctrine of jihad, and what is the character of the Islamic system of life? In this regard, the very concise yet valuable discussion of the Amir of Jamaat-e-Islami Pakistan, Sayyid Abul A'la Maududi, gives us excellent guidance. He has discussed this in his book "Jihad fi Sabil Allah". I think it is necessary to quote somewhat lengthy excerpts from this book here. For a person who wishes to understand this subject well, reading this book is absolutely essential, so that he may go into the depth of this issue, understand it properly, and grasp what role it has in establishing the Islamic movement. He says:

"Generally the word 'jihad' is translated in English as 'Holy War', and its explanation and interpretation for a long time has been carried out in such a manner that this word has come to mean 'the intoxication of madness'. On hearing it, a picture begins to move before a person's eyes that a group of religious fanatics, with drawn swords in hand, twirling their beards, with bloodthirsty eyes, is coming forward shouting 'Allahu Akbar'. Wherever they see an infidel, they seize him, place the sword on his neck and say: 'Say La ilaha illallah, otherwise your head will be separated from your body right now.' Experts have painted this picture of ours with great artistry, and beneath it have written in bold letters:
'The smell of blood comes from the people of this nation.'
The fun is that the makers of this picture are our kind benefactors who themselves for several centuries have been engaged in the extremely unholy war (Unholy War). Their own picture is that greedy for wealth and power, armed with every kind of weapon, they have pounced upon the whole world like pirates, and everywhere they search for trade markets, reserves of raw produce, lands fit for establishing colonies, and mines of minerals, so that they may supply fuel for the fire of their insatiable greed. Their war is not in the path of God but in the path of the belly. It is in the path of lust and the commanding self. For them, to attack a nation, it is enough justification that there are mines in its land, or that cotton grows there, or that oil has been discovered there, or that the goods of their factories can be well sold there, or that their surplus population can be easily settled there. If nothing else, this too is no small sin for that nation, that it lives on the road to a country which they have already occupied or now wish to occupy. As for us, what we did is a tale of past time. And their exploits are the events of the present which are passing day and night before the eyes of the world. Asia, Africa, America, in short, which part of the globe has been left which has not become a green garden through their unholy war? Yet their skill is worthy of praise. They painted our picture so badly that their own picture was hidden behind it, and our simplicity too is worthy of praise. When we saw our own picture made by others, we became so terrified that we did not even have the sense to peer behind that picture and look at the faces of the painters, and we began to apologize: 'Sir! How would we know war and fighting? We are peaceful preachers like the monks and priests. To refute some religious beliefs and to get people to accept some other beliefs, this alone is our work. What have we to do with the sword?' However, we have certainly committed this fault occasionally, that when someone came to strike us, we too raised our hand in reply. So now we have repented even of that. For the satisfaction of Your Honour, the jihad of the sword has been officially abolished. Now jihad is only the name of the effort of tongue and pen. Firing the gun is the government's work, and firing the tongue and pen is our work."

The Causes of Misunderstanding Regarding Jihad

Well, that is a matter of political maneuvers. But from a purely academic standpoint, when we analyze the causes due to which the reality of "Jihad fi Sabil Allah" has become difficult to understand, not only for non-Muslims but for Muslims themselves, we find two major and fundamental misunderstandings.

The first misunderstanding is that Islam has been regarded as a religion in the sense in which the word religion is commonly used.

The second misunderstanding is that Muslims have been regarded merely as a nation in the sense in which this word is commonly used.

These two misunderstandings have changed not only the issue of jihad alone but the whole picture of Islam as a whole, and have completely distorted the position of Muslims.

"In general terminology, what is the meaning of religion except that it is a collection of beliefs, worship and rites? In this sense, religion should indeed be a private matter. You have the freedom to hold whatever belief you wish, and your conscience may worship whatever it is pleased with, and you may call it in whatever way you like... At most, if there is any zeal and enthusiasm within you for this religion, then go about propagating your beliefs throughout the world and debate with adherents of other beliefs. What occasion is there for holding the sword in hand for this? Do you wish to make people your co-religionists by beating them? This question necessarily arises when you declare Islam to be a 'religion' in the general sense. If this is truly the position of Islam, then no justification for jihad can in reality be established."

Similarly, what is the meaning of "nation" except that it is a homogeneous group of men (A homogeneous Group of men) that, being united in some fundamental matters, has gathered together and become distinguished from other groups? In this sense, a group which is a nation takes up the sword, and can take it up, for only two reasons. Either someone attacks it to snatch its legitimate rights, or it itself attacks others to snatch their legitimate rights. In the first case, there is some degree of moral justification for taking up the sword (though some non-violent thinkers consider even this unlawful), but the second case no one can declare lawful except some dictators, and even the statesmen of vast empires like Britain and France do not today have the courage to call it lawful.

The Reality of Jihad

Therefore, if Islam is a "religion" and Muslims are a "nation", then the whole significance of jihad, on account of which it has been called the best of worships in Islam, is completely eliminated. But the reality is that Islam is not the name of a "religion", nor are Muslims the name of a "nation". Rather, Islam is a revolutionary ideology and creed which wishes to change the social order (Social Order) of the entire world and rebuild it according to its own ideology and creed. And Muslims are the name of this international revolutionary party (International Revolution Party) and of that very power which the Islamic party employs to achieve this aim.

Like all revolutionary creeds, Islam too, leaving aside common current words, adopts a special technical terminology (Terminology) so that its revolutionary concepts may be distinguished from ordinary concepts. The word jihad also belongs to this particular technical language. Islam deliberately abandoned harb and other similar Arabic words which convey the meaning of war (War), and in their place used the word "jihad", which is the equivalent of (Struggle) and even carries more emphasis than it. The correct meaning of it can be expressed in English thus:

(To exert One's Utmost endeavour in promoting a Cause) to expend all one's powers in the pursuit of a purpose.

The question is: why was this new word adopted, abandoning the old words? The answer is nothing other than that the word "war" was used, and is still used, for those battles of nations and empires which are fought for the selfish aims of individuals or groups. The motives of those battles are merely personal or collective objectives, in which not even a trace of support for any ideology or principle exists. Since the struggle of Islam is not of this nature, it altogether abandons that word. Its concern is not the interest of one nation or the interest of another nation. It has no interest in whether the rule of the earth remains with one empire or another. The thing it is concerned with is the welfare of humanity. For this welfare it holds a particular ideology and a practical creed. Wherever a government stands against this ideology and creed, Islam wishes to eliminate it, regardless of whether it is a nation or a country. Its aim is to establish the rule of its own ideology and creed, without regard to who raises its banner and whose rule is struck by it. It seeks the earth, not a part of the earth but the whole globe, not so that the rule of the earth passes from one nation or many nations into the hands of some particular nation, but only so that the whole human race may benefit from the ideology and programme of human welfare which it possesses, or, to speak more precisely, from the programme of human welfare whose name is "Islam". For this purpose it wishes to use all those forces which can be effective in bringing about revolution, and it names the collective use of all these forces "jihad". To change people's viewpoint by the power of tongue and pen and to produce a mental revolution in them is also jihad. To change the old oppressive system of life by the power of the sword and to establish a new just order is also jihad, and to spend wealth in this path and to exert the body is also jihad.

The Indispensable Qualification of "Fi Sabil Allah"

But Islam's jihad is not mere "jihad", rather it is "jihad fi sabil Allah". The qualification "fi sabil Allah" is an indispensable qualification attached to it. This phrase too belongs to that particular technical language of Islam to which I have already alluded. Its literal translation is "in the way of God". Through this translation people fell into a misunderstanding and came to think that forcing people to become followers of Islam's religious beliefs is jihad fi sabil Allah, because the meaning of "the way of God" cannot enter narrow minds in any other form. But in the language of Islam its meaning is very broad. Any work which is done for collective welfare, and whose doer's aim is not to derive any worldly benefit from it but merely to obtain the pleasure of God, Islam declares as fi sabil Allah. For example, if you give charity with the intention that some material or moral return of it comes back to you in this world, this is not fi sabil Allah. And if your intention in charity is to earn the pleasure of God by helping a poor person, then this is fi sabil Allah. Thus this terminology is specific to those works which are done with complete sincerity, purged of every kind of selfish motive, upon the conviction that a human being's working for the welfare of other human beings is a cause of God's pleasure, and that the goal of human life is nothing other than seeking the pleasure of the Master of the universe.

The qualification "fi sabil Allah" has been attached to "jihad" for this very purpose. It means that when any person or group rises to bring about a revolution in the system of life and to build a new order according to the Islamic ideology, then in this standing and this self-sacrifice and devotion there should be no selfish purpose of their own. It must in no way be their aim to remove Caesar and become Caesar themselves. Not even a trace of seeking wealth, or fame and renown, or honour and dignity for their own person should be included among the aims of their struggle. The purpose of all their sacrifices and all their efforts should be only that a just system of life be established among the servants of God. In return for this they should desire nothing but the pleasure of God. The Qur'an says:

"Those who believe fight in the way of Allah, and those who disbelieve fight in the way of Taghut." (Qur'an 4:76)

The word "taghut" derives from "tughyan", which means to go beyond the limit. When a river goes beyond its limit, you say that a flood has come. Similarly, when a man goes beyond his lawful limit and uses his power for the purpose of becoming a god over human beings or of gaining excessive benefits beyond his due share, this is fighting in the way of taghut.

And in contrast, a war in the way of God is one whose sole aim is that the law of God's justice be established in the world, that the fighter himself also abide by it, and that he also enforce its observance upon others. Accordingly, the Qur'an says:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 8, verse 1 (part 3 of 3):

﴿That is the Last Abode. We shall assign it to those who do not desire haughtiness in the earth, nor corruption. And the good end is for the God-fearing.﴾ Surely, We have reserved the station of honour in the Hereafter only for those who do not wish to establish their greatness in the earth and to cause corruption. The success of the final outcome is only for the God-fearing people.

In a hadith it has come that a man asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "What is meant by fighting in the way of Allah? One man fights for booty. Another fights to gain a reputation for bravery. A third person fights because he bears enmity toward someone, or because the fervour of tribal zeal moves him. Whose fighting is in the way of Allah?" The Prophet (ﷺ) replied: "None of them. Fighting in the way of Allah is only the fighting of the one who has no aim other than making the word of Allah supreme."

In another hadith it is stated: "If someone fights, and in his heart there is even the intention of obtaining a single rope for tying a camel, then his reward is lost." Allah accepts only that deed which is done purely for His pleasure, with no personal or collective purpose in view. Therefore, the restriction "in the way of Allah" in jihad carries special importance from the Islamic standpoint. Mere fighting is done by every living being in the world. Each one exerts his full strength to achieve his goal. But "Muslim" is the name of a revolutionary community, and among its revolutionary ideas one of the most important, indeed the fundamental, idea is this: spend your life and wealth, fight against all the rebellious powers of the world, expend all the powers of your body and soul, so that you may displace the other rebels and take their place, but rather solely so that rebellion and tyranny are erased from the world and the law of Allah is enforced in the world.

After briefly stating this meaning of jihad and this significance of "in the way of Allah," I wish to offer a brief explanation of the revolutionary call that Islam brought, so that it may be easily understood what need there is for jihad for this call and what its objective is.

**The Islamic Revolutionary Call**

The summary of the Islamic revolutionary call is this:

﴿O mankind, worship your Lord who created you.﴾ O people! Worship only your Lord who created you.

Islam does not call upon labourers, landlords, farmers or factory owners, but calls upon all human beings. Its address is to man as man, and it says that if you serve, obey and submit to anyone other than God, then abandon that. If within yourselves there is the impulse of divinity, remove it from your minds too. For no one among you has the right to have others serve him or to make others bow their heads before him. You must all accept the worship of one God, and in that worship all of you must stand on one level.

﴿Come to a word that is equal between us and you: that we worship none but Allah, and that we associate nothing with Him, and that some of us do not take others as lords besides Allah.﴾ Come, let us and you gather upon a matter that is common between us and you: that we shall not serve anyone except Allah, nor associate anything with Him in His divinity, nor shall any of us make another a lord in place of Allah, holding the authority of command and prohibition.

This was the call of a universal and comprehensive revolution. It proclaimed aloud: ﴿Judgement belongs only to Allah.﴾ Sovereignty belongs to none but Allah. No one has the right to become by his own self a ruler of human beings and to command whatever he wishes by his own authority and forbid whatever he wishes. To regard any human being as possessing command and prohibition in his own right is in fact to make him a partner in divinity. And in the world this is the very root of corruption. The reason why people deviate from the correct nature upon which Allah created man, and from the straight path of living which He showed him, is simply that people forget God and, as a consequence, also forget their own reality. The inevitable outcome of this is that on one side some individuals, families or classes rise with an open or hidden claim to divinity and, by exploiting their power unlawfully, make people their servants. And on the other side, the result of this self-sale to God and self-forgetfulness is that a section of the people accepts the divinity of the powerful and acknowledges their right to command, while these others bow their heads before that command. This is the foundation of oppression, corruption and unlawful exploitation in the world, and Islam strikes its first blow precisely here. It proclaims openly: ﴿And do not obey the command of the extravagant, who cause corruption in the earth and do not reform.﴾ Do not at all obey the command of those people who have exceeded their lawful limits and spread corruption in the earth and do not set things right.

﴿Do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his own desire, and whose affair is excess.﴾ Do not at all obey the one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who has become a slave of his own carnal desires, and whose affairs are based on excess and deficiency.

﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers, who hinder from the path of Allah and seek to make it crooked.﴾ The curse of Allah is upon those wrongdoers who place obstacles in the straight path of life which God has laid down, and wish to make it crooked.

It asks people: ﴿Are many scattered lords better, or Allah, the One, the Irresistible?﴾ Are these many small gods, in whose servitude you are being crushed, acceptable to you, or the One God who is the most mighty? If you do not accept the worship of this one God, you will never be freed from the lordship of these small and false gods. They will somehow gain dominion over you and will certainly create corruption: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town, they ruin it and make the honourable of its people abject; and thus do they do.﴾ When these kings enter a town, they overturn its system of life and humiliate its people of honour, and this is their practice.

﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the earth to cause corruption therein and to destroy the crops and the offspring; and Allah does not love corruption.﴾ And when he attains power, he spreads corruption in the earth, destroys the fields and ruins the generations, and Allah does not love corruption.

Here there is no room for full detail. Briefly, I wish to make clear to you that the call of Islam to the unity of God and the worship of God was not, in the sense in which religious calls generally are, merely a call to a religious creed. In reality it was a call to a social revolution. Its blow fell directly upon those classes which, in a religious guise as priests, or in a political guise as kings, chiefs and ruling groups, or in an economic guise as moneylenders, landlords and monopolists, had made the common people their servants. Openly, they were the lords besides Allah. They demanded obedience and servitude from people on the basis of their inherited or class rights, and they plainly said: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾, ﴿I am your highest lord﴾, ﴿I give life and cause death﴾, and ﴿Who is stronger than us in power?﴾ And in some places, in order to exploit the ignorance of the common people, they had set up artificial gods in the form of idols and temples, behind whose cover they claimed their divine rights from the servants of God. Therefore, Islam's call against unbelief, polytheism and idol-worship, and its preaching for the worship and servitude of the One God, directly clashed with the interests of the government and of the classes that supported it or moved on its support. For this reason, whenever any prophet or people raised the cry ﴿Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾, the government of the time immediately stood up against it, and all the classes that profited unlawfully took up arms in opposition. Because this was not merely a statement of a metaphysical proposition, but the proclamation of a social revolution, and in that first call the scent of political turmoil was immediately detected.

**The Distinctive Feature of the Islamic Revolutionary Call**

There is no doubt that all the prophets (peace be upon them) were revolutionary leaders, and Sayyidina Muhammad (ﷺ) is the greatest revolutionary leader. But what draws a clear line of distinction between ordinary revolutionaries of the world and these God-fearing revolutionary leaders is this: other revolutionaries, however good their intentions may be, cannot attain the correct position of justice and moderation. Either they do not rise from among the oppressed classes themselves, or they rise with a spirit of supporting them and then view all matters from the standpoint of those same classes. The natural result is that their view is not an impartial and pure view of humanity, but one that carries anger and hatred toward one class and sympathy toward another. They think of a cure for oppression which in its outcome becomes a counter-oppression. For them it is not possible, free from the emotions of revenge, envy and enmity, to devise a balanced and moderate social system in which the welfare of all human beings as a whole is secured. By contrast, the prophets (peace be upon them), however much they were persecuted and however much oppression was inflicted upon them and their companions, never allowed their personal feelings to enter their revolutionary movement. They worked directly under the guidance of God, and since God is free from human emotions, has no particular relationship with any human class, and holds no grievance or enmity against any other human class, therefore under the guidance of God the prophets (peace be upon them) viewed all matters with unbiased justice, asking what lies in the collective welfare and wellbeing of all human beings. How a system can be established in which every person can remain within his lawful limits, enjoy his lawful rights, and in which there may be complete balance in the mutual relations of individuals and in the relationship between the individual and the community. For this reason, the revolutionary movement of the prophets (peace be upon them) never turned into class war. They did not carry out social reconstruction in such a way as to impose one class upon another, but adopted a method of justice in which equal possibilities of progress and material and spiritual felicity were kept open for all human beings.

(Owing to its great length, the complete commentary on this verse could not be included. We apologise for this. Please read the remainder of the commentary of this verse in Fi Zilal al-Quran.)

(Section three of the surah introduction)

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent ʿAmmar ibn Yasir and ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud to gather information about the enemy. They circled the enemy's encampment and, on returning, reported to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that the enemy was greatly distressed and that rain was falling heavily upon them.

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ halted at the well, a platform was made for him of palm branches, and Saʿd ibn Muʿadh stood at its entrance with his sword drawn. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ toured the battlefield, and he pointed out to his companions the place where each of the chiefs of the Quraysh would be slain. He would say, "Here will be slain so-and-so, here will be slain so-and-so." And they were all slain, and not one of them went beyond the spot the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had designated. Then he ﷺ straightened the ranks of the Muslims and returned to his platform. Only Abu Bakr was with him.

Ibn Ishaq says: The Quraysh travelled the whole night and by morning came face to face for battle. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw the Quraysh, he turned away from the hill, turned his face toward the valley, and at that time made this supplication: "O Allah, here is the tribe of Quraysh, advancing with great arrogance and pride, opposing You and denying Your Messenger. Today I seek Your help, the help You promised me. O Allah, destroy them tomorrow." While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was saying this, his gaze fell upon ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, who was riding a red camel. He was with the Quraysh. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If there is any goodness among the people of Quraysh, it can only be with the rider of the red camel."

Hakim ibn Hizam narrates that Hafaf ibn Ima ibn Rahdah al-Ghifari, or his father Ima, sent some livestock for slaughter to the people of Quraysh through his son, along with a message that if they wished, they could also be given weapons and men for support. The Quraysh thanked him through his son and said that he had fulfilled the right of kinship and had discharged his obligation toward them. They said: "By God, if we have set out to fight men, we feel no weakness before men. And if our fight is against God, as Muhammad believes, then no one has any strength against God."

When the people reached their destination, some people came to draw water from the pool that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had prepared. Among them was Hakim ibn Hizam. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Let them drink water." Thus, everyone who drank from that pool was killed, except Hakim ibn Hizam. He later became a Muslim and became a very good Muslim, and whenever he took an oath and emphasized it, he would say: "By the God who saved me on the day of Badr."

Ibn Ishaq says: Abu Ishaq ibn Yasar al-Jumahi and other elders of the Ansar told me that when the people of Quraysh had settled down comfortably, they sent ʿUmayr ibn Wahb al-Jumahi to estimate the companions of Muhammad and report whether the Muslim army had any hidden force or reinforcements. It is said that he went around the valley twice, far and wide, saw nothing, and on returning reported: "I have found no trace. But O people of Quraysh, I see a calamity in which many people will die. Death is clearly visible in the flashing of Yathrib's swords. We face a people whose defence and whose fortress are only their swords. By God, I do not think any of them will be killed unless they kill one of us. If they kill as many of us as they are in number, then there will be no pleasure for us in remaining alive. Therefore, it is appropriate that you all think carefully about this war."

When Hakim ibn Hizam heard these words, he went around among the people, and first met ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah. He said: "O Abu al-Walid, you are the elder and chief of the Quraysh, and your word carries weight among them. Would it not be fitting that your people remember one of your good deeds until the Day of Resurrection?" He said: "Hakim, what is that good deed?" Hakim said: "The good deed is that you lead the people back, and that the matter of your ally ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami be placed upon you." He replied: "I accept this. You are my witness to it. He is my ally, so his blood-money will be my responsibility" (that is, the blood-money for his brother who was killed by the Muslims in the expedition of ʿAbdullah ibn Jahsh). "Also, whatever property the Muslims took from him is my responsibility too. But it is appropriate that you go to the son of Hanzaliyyah, because I fear that because of him differences will arise among the people." By this he meant Abu Jahl.

After this, ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah gave a speech: "O people of Quraysh, by God, what will you gain from Muhammad and the companions of Muhammad? If you kill them, no one among you will want to look at the one he has killed, for his slain man will be his cousin, his maternal cousin, or someone from his own family. Therefore, it is appropriate that you return and let Muhammad and all the Arabs contend with each other. If the Arabs kill him, your purpose is fulfilled; and if the situation turns out otherwise, you will meet him in a state in which you have not treated him in this way."

After this speech, I came to Abu Jahl. I saw that he had taken his armour out of its bag and was preparing it. I said to him: "O Abu al-Hakam, ʿUtbah has sent me to you with these proposals." He replied that ʿUtbah's faculties had been disturbed upon seeing Muhammad and his companions; such a thing could never happen. He said: "By God, we will not return until Allah decides between us and Muhammad. And what ʿUtbah says is because he has seen that Muhammad and his companions are slaughtering animals and eating, and among them is his son Abu Hudhayfah, who has become a Muslim, and ʿUtbah fears that they will be killed by the army of Quraysh."

After that, he sent a message to ʿAmir al-Hadrami: "Look, ʿUtbah is your ally, and he wants to lead the people back, although you have seen your prey with your own eyes. So remind him and your covenant, and remind the people that your brothers have already been killed." Thereupon ʿAmir al-Hadrami stood up, stripped himself bare, and cried out: "Alas, ʿAmr!" War then broke out, and the battle grew fierce among the people. They became resolute in the strife they had decided upon, and the matter that ʿUtbah had been calling the people to was forgotten. When ʿUtbah learned that Abu Jahl was saying these things, he said that soon it would become known who was frightened, the yellowness of his buttocks would reveal whether it was his or mine.

Ibn Ishaq says that Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad al-Makhzumi was an extremely bold and ill-tempered man. He said: "By God, I will drink from their pool, or I will destroy it, or I will be killed at the pool." When he came out, Hamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib advanced toward him. When Hamzah struck him, he cut off one of his legs. He was then near the pool. He fell on his back, and blood spurted from his leg toward his companions, but he crawled on his belly toward the pool and went into it. His aim was to fulfil his oath, but Hamzah pursued him and, with a single blow, killed him inside the pool.

After that, ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah came out, with his brother Shaybah and his son Walid ibn ʿUtbah. When they separated from their line, they called for single combat. From the Ansar, three young men advanced to face them: ʿAwf and Muʿawwidh, the sons of al-Harith, whose mother was ʿAfra, and a third man, ʿAbdullah ibn Rawahah. The group of ʿUtbah asked: "Who are you?" They said: "We are Ansar." ʿUtbah said: "We have no business with you." In Ibn Ishaq's narration, ʿUtbah told those Ansari men: "You are our honourable equals, but our purpose is to fight our own brothers." Then they called out: "O Muhammad, bring forward against us men of our own standing from our people." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then said: "ʿUbaydah ibn al-Harith, Hamzah and ʿAli, go forth." When they came out and drew near to ʿUtbah's group, they asked the same question: "Who are you?" ʿUbaydah said: "I am ʿUbaydah." Hamzah said: "I am Hamzah." ʿAli said: "I am ʿAli." They said: "Yes, you are honourable equals." ʿUbaydah, who was advanced in years, challenged ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah to single combat; Hamzah challenged Shaybah ibn Rabiʿah; and ʿAli challenged Walid ibn ʿUtbah. Hamzah finished off Shaybah with a single blow, and ʿAli killed Walid with a single blow. Between ʿUbaydah and ʿUtbah there were two exchanges of blows, and they wounded each other so badly that neither could move from his place. But ʿAli and Hamzah turned toward ʿUtbah, finished his work, and carried their companion back to their camp.

Now the people advanced and the battle began. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had instructed his companions not to attack until he ordered them, and if the enemy attacked, to defend themselves with their spears. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ straightened the ranks and returned to his platform. He went inside, and at that time only Abu Bakr was with him, and no one else. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was calling upon his Lord and reminding Him of the promise concerning victory made to him. Among other things, at that moment of supplication he said: "O Allah, if this small band is destroyed today, You will never be worshipped." Abu Bakr was saying: "Reduce your supplication. Allah will surely fulfil His promise."

In al-Imta' al-Isma' of al-Maqrizi it is mentioned that ʿAbdullah ibn Rawahah said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "O Messenger, I give you this advice, although you have no need of advice: that Allah has no need to be reminded of His promises." Upon this, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Ibn Rawahah, should I not remind Allah of His promise? Allah is the One who fulfils His promises and never goes against them."

Ibn Ishaq said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in the platform, slumber overcame him briefly. When he awoke, he said: "Be glad, Abu Bakr, the help of Allah has come. Here is Jibril leading his horse by its bridle, and dust is rising on both sides of it."

A freed slave of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), Mihja', was struck by an arrow and became a martyr. He was the first of the Muslims to be killed. After that, Harithah ibn Suraqah shot a man of the Banu ʿAdi ibn al-Najjar and killed him. That man was drinking water from the pool. The arrow struck his neck, and he became a martyr.

After that, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came out of the platform and urged the people to fight. He said: "By God, whoever fights today for the sake of Allah with patience and steadfastness, advancing and not turning his back, will certainly enter Paradise."

A man, ʿUmayr ibn al-Hammam, a brother of Banu Salamah, was eating dates at that time. He heard the words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "Excellent! O Messenger, is there only this much distance between me and Paradise, that these people should kill me?" Then he threw away the dates, took up his sword, and fought fiercely until he became a martyr.

Ibn Ishaq has narrated this report: a man, ʿAwf ibn al-Harith, who was the son of "ʿAfra," asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at what deed Allah laughs at His servant. He said: "Allah laughs when a man goes into the ranks of the enemy with a sword, without any armour on his body." So he took off the armour he was wearing, threw it away, took up his sword, went into the ranks of the enemy, and fought until he became a martyr.

Ibn Ishaq narrated from al-Zuhri that when the two sides drew near each other, Abu Jahl said: "O Allah, whoever among us is the more severe in cutting family ties, and whoever does what is not known as good, then defeat him tomorrow." And so his supplication was answered.

Ibn Ishaq narrates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took a handful of dust, threw it toward the Quraysh, and said: "Shahat al-wujuh" (May the faces be disfigured), and told his companions to press on. After this, the opponents were defeated; most of the chiefs of the Quraysh were killed, and the rest were taken captive.

When the people stopped killing and began taking captives, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw signs of displeasure on the face of Saʿd ibn Muʿadh, because people were taking opponents captive instead of killing them, he addressed him and said: "By God, and perhaps you dislike what these people are doing."

He said: "Yes, Sir, I dislike it. This is the first battle in which truth and falsehood have clashed. I consider that thoroughly crushing the enemy in this battle would have been better for us than taking them captive."

Ibn Ishaq narrates a report from Hazrat Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) instructed his Companions: "Some people from Banu Hashim have come with this army under compulsion, and they do not want to fight against us. So whoever among you encounters anyone from Banu Hashim should not kill him. And whoever finds Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham ibn al-Harith ibn Asad should also not kill him. And whoever finds Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib should also not kill him, for Hazrat Abbas has come with the army under compulsion." Upon this, Abu Hudhayfah ibn Utbah ibn Rabi'ah (who was a Muslim) said: "Shall we kill our fathers, brothers, sons and family, and leave Abbas? By Allah, if I find him, I will make him taste (the sword)." This statement reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said to Hazrat Umar ibn al-Khattab: "O Abu Hafs!" (This was the first day that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed me with this kunyah.) "Shall the face of the Messenger of Allah's uncle be struck with the sword?" Upon this, Hazrat Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, permit me to strike off his neck. By Allah, he is a hypocrite." After this conversation, Abu Hudhayfah used to say: "The words I spoke on that occasion, I fear them to this day, and I will always continue to fear them, unless I atone for them by being martyred." Later, Abu Hudhayfah was martyred in the battle against the apostates on the Day of Yamamah.

Ibn Ishaq says that the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the killing of Abu al-Bakhtari because, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was in Makkah, he used to restrain people from harassing him. He had never heard anything from the Prophet (ﷺ) that would have caused him distress. He was also among those who broke the pact that the Quraysh had written to boycott Banu Hashim. But on that day he was killed because he refused to be taken as a prisoner.

Ibn Ishaq narrates from Yahya ibn Abbad that his father said: "Umayyah ibn Khalaf was my friend, and my name in the Jahiliyyah was Abd Amr. When I accepted Islam, I took the name Abd al-Rahman. At that time we were in Makkah. Umayyah would call me, 'Abd Amr,' and say, 'You have abandoned the name by which your father named you.' I would say, 'Yes.' He would say, 'I do not know al-Rahman, so choose for me a name of our own, so that I may call you by it, because you do not respond when I call you by the first name, and I do not use the second name, which I do not know.' When he called me 'Abd Amr,' I would not answer. I told him, 'You choose a name for me.' So he named me Abd al-Ilah. When we met, he would call me 'Abd al-Ilah,' and we would converse. On the day of Badr, I saw him standing with his son Ali ibn Umayyah, and I was carrying some armor that I had taken as spoils after the battle. When he saw me, he said, 'O Abd Amr!' and I did not respond. Then he said, 'O Abd al-Ilah!' and I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Do you have any interest in us? I think I will be more beneficial to you than the armor you are carrying.' I said, 'Yes.' So I threw down the armor, and I took hold of both of them by the hand and made them prisoners. He said, 'I have never seen a day like this. Do you not need milk?' That is, he meant that he would give me milking camels as ransom, for whoever had taken him prisoner. I took them with me to the camp."

Ibn Ishaq narrates that Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf said: "Umayyah ibn Khalaf told me, while I was between him and his son and I was holding the hands of both of them: 'Abd al-Ilah, which of you was the man who had ostrich feathers on his chest?' I said, 'That is Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib.' He said, 'This man has done severe deeds against us.'"

Abd al-Rahman says: "By Allah, while I was taking these people along, suddenly Bilal saw him with me. This was the same man who used to torment Bilal and force him to renounce Islam in Makkah. He would take him out to the desert of Makkah. When the sand became hot, he would lay him on his back, then place a large stone on his chest, and then say, 'You will remain like this until you abandon the religion of Muhammad.' And Bilal would keep saying, 'Ahad, Ahad.' When Bilal saw him, he cried out, 'This is the chief of the disbelievers, Umayyah ibn Khalaf! If he escapes, I will not be saved!' I said, 'Bilal, do you do this to my prisoner?' He said again, 'If he is saved, it is as if I am not saved.' I said again, sternly, 'O son of the black woman, do you not listen?' He said again, 'If he is saved, I am dead.' Then, it is said, Bilal called out in a very loud voice, 'O Ansar of Allah! This is the chief of the disbelievers, Umayyah ibn Khalaf! If he escapes, I am finished.' It is said that people surrounded us, but I kept restraining people from the two of them. From behind, a man came and struck his son, and he fell. Then Umayyah ibn Khalaf let out a shriek. Upon this I said, 'Save yourself so that I may also be saved, for by Allah, I can do nothing now.' It is said that people struck him with swords repeatedly until they were finished with him. Abd al-Rahman used to say: 'May Allah have mercy on Bilal, for my armor was lost and he also distressed me by killing my prisoners.'"

Ibn Ishaq says that when the Prophet (ﷺ) finished with the enemy, he ordered that Abu Jahl be searched for among the dead. As is related in the narrations, Mu'adh ibn Amr ibn al-Jamuh, the brother of Banu Salamah, said: "I heard people say that reaching Abu Jahl was very difficult, and that he was then behind a tree. When I heard this, I resolved to do this task. I moved toward him, and when it was possible for me, I attacked him. I struck him with a blow that severed his leg at half the shin. When his leg was cut off, I felt as if a date stone was flying out from under a stone that crushes date stones. After that blow, his son Ikrimah struck me, and a blow hit my shoulder so that my arm was cut off and hung from one side at my side by the skin. Then the fighting became more intense and hurried. I paid no attention to it and kept fighting the whole day, and this hand remained hanging behind my back. When it troubled me greatly, I placed my foot on it, cut it off, and threw it away."

After that, Mu'awwidh ibn Afra reached Abu Jahl, and at that time his leg was cut off. He wounded him so severely that he could no longer move. Mu'awwidh kept fighting until he was killed. After that, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud reached Abu Jahl. This happened when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had ordered that Abu Jahl be searched for among the dead. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had told those searching: "Look for him. If you have difficulty recognizing him, then look at his knee, for there is a wound on it. This is because he and I once attended a feast at the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an, and at that time we were both boys. In the crowd, I pushed him, and although I was thin compared to him, he fell to his knees. One of his knees was injured so badly that the effects of the wound never disappeared." Hazrat Abdullah ibn Mas'ud says: "I found him in a state where he was taking his last breaths. I placed my foot on his neck. Once in Makkah, he had mistreated me. He had struck me and had made my ... (marks)." Then I said to him: "O enemy of Allah, have you realized that today Allah has humiliated you?" He said: "Why have you humiliated me? Have you killed a man greater than me?" He also said: "Tell me, who won the battle today?" I replied: "Allah and His Messenger have won."

Ibn Ishaq says that some people of Banu Makhzum used to think that Ibn Mas'ud said that Abu Jahl told him: "O shepherd, you are riding on the neck of a great man, which is not an easy thing to ride." It is said that after this, I cut off his neck from his body and brought it and placed it at the feet of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and said: "O Messenger of Allah, here is the head of the enemy of Allah." Upon this, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) thanked Allah.

Ibn Hisham says that the learned experts of Maqami narrated to me that Hazrat Umar ibn al-Khattab once said to Sa'id ibn al-As: "I think you have a misunderstanding about me, that perhaps I killed your father. If I had killed him, I would never have apologized for his killing. But I killed my maternal uncle, al-As ibn Hisham ibn al-Mughirah. As for your father, I passed by him in the battle, and he was fighting the way a bull tears up the ground with its horns. So I stepped aside from him, and his cousin moved ahead of me, confronted him, and killed him."

Ibn Ishaq, Yazid ibn Ruman, and Urwah ibn al-Zubayr narrate through Hazrat Aisha that when the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that the dead be thrown into a pit, a pit was dug and all of them were thrown into it, except Umayyah ibn Khalaf, because he had swollen inside his armor and had filled the armor. People went to him and moved him, and his flesh separated from his body. The people left him in that place and covered him with dirt. When all the dead had been placed in the pit, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood at the edge of the pit and said: "O people of the pit, have you seen the outcome that your Lord promised you? I have seen the outcome that my Lord promised me, completely." It is said that the Companions of the Messenger asked him: "You are speaking to dead people?" He said: "The truth is that they now know that the promise their Lord made to them was true." Hazrat Aisha says: "People say that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, they hear what I say.'" But the Prophet (ﷺ) had actually said: "In truth, they know that the Lord's promise was true."

Ibn Ishaq says that when the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that they be thrown into the pit, Utbah ibn Rabi'ah was dragged toward the pit, and the Prophet (ﷺ) looked at him. (This has reached me.) Abu Hudhayfah ibn Utbah was extremely grieved and his color had changed. So the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Abu Hudhayfah, perhaps something has affected you because of your father?" Or the words the Prophet (ﷺ) said were like this. Abu Hudhayfah said: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, it is not so! I have no doubt about my father, nor about his killing. But I knew that my father was a very prudent, forbearing and knowledgeable man, and my heart's desire was that Allah would guide him to Islam. When I saw his condition, and it occurred to me that he had departed in a state of disbelief, and my wish had not been fulfilled, this caused me grief." Upon this, the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed good for his father and also spoke very good words about him.

After this, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that everything in the camp be gathered together. All the spoils were brought together. Disagreement arose among the Muslims about this. Those who had collected the goods said: "The whole of it is our right, because we collected it." Those who were striking the enemy and pursuing them said: "If we had not been there, where would you have gathered it? We kept the enemy occupied, while you collected the goods." And those who were assigned to protect the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We protected the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the enemy's attack. Therefore our right is greater than yours. We saw these goods at that time, but there was no guard for you. We feared that if we left, the enemy would attack you. So we remained in protection. Therefore, you are no more deserving than we are."

Ibn Ishaq says that Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith and others narrated from Sulayman, Makhul, and Abu Umamah al-Bahili. They said: "I asked Hazrat Ubadah ibn al-Samit about the Anfal (spoils), and he said: 'This surah was revealed concerning us, the Companions of Badr. At that time, disagreements arose among us about the Anfal, and our moral condition regarding it was not good. Therefore Allah took the Anfal away from us and placed it under the authority of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) distributed it equally among the Muslims.'"

Ibn Ishaq says that Nubayh ibn Wahb, a brother of Banu Abd al-Dar, reported that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned to the prisoners, he distributed them among his Companions, and he instructed them to treat the prisoners well. Abu Aziz ibn Hashim, a full brother of Mus'ab ibn Umayr, was among the prisoners. Abu Aziz related: "An Ansari was taking me captive, and Mus'ab ibn Umayr, my brother, came and said to the Ansari: 'Tie him up well, for his mother is a wealthy woman, and she will pay a large ransom for him.'" He said: "When they brought me from the battlefield, I was with the Ansar. When it was time for food, they would give me bread, while they themselves would be content with dates. Whoever received bread would give it to me. I would feel ashamed and return it to them, but they would give it back to me and would not even touch it."

Ibn Hisham says: Abu Aziz was the standard-bearer of the polytheists on the day of Badr, and this standard had come to him after Nadr ibn al-Harith. When Abu al-Yasar, who had captured him, was told by Mus'ab ibn Umayr what has been mentioned above, Abu Aziz said: "O brother, you are recommending me on this matter?" Mus'ab said: "This Ansari is your brother before you." Upon this, his mother enquired what the highest ransom of any Quraysh was, and she was told that it was four thousand dirhams. So she sent four thousand dirhams and paid his ransom.

Ibn Ishaq says: after this, the Quraysh sent the ransom for their captives.

----

This was the factual outline of the Battle of Badr; we have tried, to the extent of our ability, to narrate it briefly. Surah al-Anfal was revealed as a commentary on this battle. In it there is comment on the outward events of this battle, and mention of its historical background too. All these comments are in the unique and miraculous style of the Qur'an, the details of which we shall set out in the course of explaining the verses ahead. Here we have only given, briefly, the basic outline of this surah's themes.

On what line does this surah proceed? One theme fully clarifies it. Ibn Ishaq narrated from Hadrat Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said that this surah was revealed concerning the people of Badr: when we began to disagree among ourselves about the spoils of war, and our conduct in this matter also deteriorated, Allah took the authority over the spoils (anfal) out of our hands and gave it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he distributed the spoils according to the principle of equality.

This narration shows how this surah began and what its line is. People disagreed about the spoils acquired in this event, which Allah Most High made a Furqan (criterion) for human history until the Day of Resurrection.

Allah intended to give them, and those who would come after them, certain important teachings. This teaching was fully given here, and the wisdom and the decree of destiny by which Allah gave this teaching is such that every step appears to have a corrective purpose behind it. For the Battle of Badr and the great decisions that resulted from it, the planning of the Muslims themselves had no role. They had made no plan regarding the spoils of the minor booty of Badr, nor had they considered the great results of that battle. All these affairs happened through Allah's will and plan. In this event Allah tested the Muslims thoroughly, and this was His grace and kindness.

Allah Most High told what people thought about themselves. They thought they would plunder the caravan, but Allah brought an armed army against them in place of the caravan. See how great the difference is, so that people might see how influential their own thinking was, and how far-reaching the wisdom of Allah's plan regarding them is, and how great the difference between the two is.

The surah begins with a question from the people about the anfal, and a brief answer from Allah that these spoils belong to Allah and His Messenger. After this it is said that they should fear God and mend their mutual relations, as Hadrat Ubadah ibn al-Samit said that their conduct had been affected; they should remove this and obey Allah and the Messenger of Allah, because submission and obedience are the requirement of faith. At the beginning of the surah, a most impressive portrayal is made of the believers:

﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger. So fear Allah, set right your mutual relations, and obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers. The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and when His verses are recited to them they increase them in faith, and they put their trust in their Lord; who establish prayer and spend out of what We have provided them. It is these who are truly believers; for them are degrees with their Lord, forgiveness and a generous provision.﴾ (Al-Anfal, verses 1–4)

After this, the matter of Badr is brought to mind. It is told what they were thinking for themselves, and what Allah was planning for them, and what they were seeing on earth according to worldly standards, and what the decree of Allah's destiny was doing:

﴿Just as your Lord brought you forth from your house in truth, though a party of the believers were averse, they disputed with you concerning the truth after it had become clear, as if they were being driven to death while they looked on. And when Allah promised you that one of the two parties would be yours, and you wished that the one without thorns would be yours, but Allah willed to establish the truth by His words and to cut off the root of the disbelievers; that He might establish truth and nullify falsehood, even though the guilty disliked it.﴾

(Because of its great length, the complete commentary on this verse could not be included. We apologise for this. Please read the remainder of the commentary on this verse in Fi Zilal al-Quran.)

**Lesson 83: At a Glance**

This is the first lesson of this surah. Its subject is the *anfal* (the bounties, i.e. additional gains and special portions reserved by the leader) and the distribution of *ghanimah* (war booty). Anfal and ghanimah include everything that Muslims obtain on the battlefield when the fighting is *jihad fi sabilillah* (struggle in the way of Allah). The first dispute over the distribution of booty arose among the people of Badr. Allah turned the believers' attention to the matters of fear of Allah and obedience to the Messenger, and the feelings of faith and *taqwa* (God-consciousness) were stirred in their hearts.

Allah reminded them: "You had from the outset wished to attack the caravan and gain booty, but Allah's wisdom required that He bestow on you victory and honour." Then He told them to reflect on the stages of that battle: your numbers and equipment were very few compared with the enemy's, and they were far superior to you. Yet Allah strengthened your feet through the angels. Then He sent rain, which made fighting easier for you. Your feet were firmly planted, you were watering your livestock with the rainwater and bathing, because the battle of Badr was fought on sand, and in sand the feet of men and horses sink. Then you were reminded that a kind of sleep overtook you, and as soon as you slept you became tranquil. Then Allah cast terror into the hearts of your enemies and sent down a severe punishment upon them.

In the light of these experiences, the Qur'an commands you to show steadfastness in every battle, even though the strength of the enemy may seem greater to you outwardly, because it is Allah who actually kills. It is Allah who in reality shoots the arrow, and it is He who governs affairs. You are in truth only a veil for the decree of Allah; He drives you as He wills. After this, the lesson comments on the foolish behaviour of the polytheists, who before that event had prayed before Allah: "O Allah, if this party is in error and cuts off the ties of kinship, then destroy it in today's battle." Allah says: ﴿If you were seeking a decision, then the decision has come to you﴾.

The Muslims are told to remove hypocrisy from their lives and not to adopt the attitude of the hypocrites, who said, "We hear," but did not truly hear, because when they heard they did not accept.

At the end of this lesson, the Muslims are repeatedly called upon: "O believers! When the Messenger calls you, respond to him, because he gives you a call through which you will attain everlasting life, even though outwardly he may be calling you to death and slaughter." Allah reminds the believers to remember the time when you were few and weak, and were always afraid, on every side, that the enemy would snatch you away. In those circumstances Allah gave you refuge and support. And now there is a promise for you: if you adopt the path of *taqwa*, Allah will grant you decisive conduct and a decisive judgment, will forgive your sins, will overlook your shortcomings, and what Allah has prepared for you in the Hereafter is far greater than all the spoils and wealth of this world.
