Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verses 9 to 14:

Now, within the context, one of the scenes of this decisive battle is presented. From this scene it becomes clear what condition the community of believers was in at that time, what measures Allah adopted for them, and that the help and support of Allah reached them solely by the Divine will and Divine aid. The matchless style of the Qur'an records the observations, impressions, events, anxieties and hopes of this encounter with great precision, in such a way that the reader feels as though he himself is within this battle, yet with Qur'anic commentary, so that they may understand the realities within a wider circle than Badr. Their view should be broader than the Arabian Peninsula, indeed their outlook should be wider than the entire universe. In this discourse, the background of this battle now extends to the Exalted Assembly (al-Mala' al-A'la). Now this battle goes beyond the Day of Badr, beyond the whole of human history, and reaches the Hereafter, which is wider than the sphere of worldly life. In this foreground the community of believers is made aware of its worth in the sight of Allah, how important its deeds are, and how sacred its struggle and movement for the establishment of the Din is.

This is a battle which is proceeding in accordance with the command and will of Allah. The system of qada' and qadr of Allah and His planning are themselves at work. Special contingents of Allah are participating in it. In this battle, the scenes of the movement of the battlefield, its dangers and its successes are clearly visible in the Qur'anic expressions. This is a living scene, and it appears as though it is still before one's eyes.

The question is: what was the supplication of the believers in this battle? Imam Ahmad narrates from Hadrat Umar ibn al-Khattab: when the event of Badr arose, the Prophet ﷺ looked at his companions and saw that they were a little over three hundred; and when he looked at the disbelievers, he found that they were a little over one thousand. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned his blessed face towards the qiblah, he was wearing a cloak and a waist-wrapper, and said: "O Allah, fulfil what You have promised me. O Allah, if today You destroy this small band of the people of Islam, then never again will You be worshipped on earth." It is said that he continued to beseech and call upon Allah in this manner until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Hadrat Abu Bakr came, took hold of the cloak, placed it back on his shoulders, held it from behind, and then said: "O Prophet of Allah, your supplication to Allah is sufficient; surely Allah will fulfil His promise." Upon this, Allah revealed these verses.

"Idh tastaghithuna rabbakum fastajaba lakum anni mumiddukum bi-alfin mina al-mala'ikati murdifin" (8:9): And [remember] when you were seeking help from your Lord, and He responded to you: "Indeed, I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another." Concerning the number of angels on the Day of Badr and their manner of fighting, numerous and detailed narrations have come down, and they describe what the angels said to the believers, how they encouraged them, and what they said to the disbelievers and how they humiliated them. However, in accordance with our method in Zilal al-Qur'an, we content ourselves with this, because this matter relates to the unseen realm and the texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah concerning it are clear. Here the Qur'anic verses are entirely clear, for example:

"Idh tastaghithuna rabbakum fastajaba lakum anni mumiddukum bi-alfin mina al-mala'ikati murdifin" (8:9): And [remember] when you were seeking help from your Lord, and He responded to you: "Indeed, I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another." This was their number. And their manner of fighting was this:

"Idh yuhi rabbuka ila al-mala'ikati anni ma'akum fa-thabbitu alladhina amanu, sa-ulqi fi qulubi alladhina kafaru al-ru'b fa-idribu fawqa al-a'naqi wa-idribu minhum kulla banan" (8:12): And [remember] when your Lord inspired the angels: "Indeed I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved; so strike [them] upon the necks and strike every fingertip of them."

This was their practical task. There is absolutely no need for further detail on this, since the verse is clear in its meaning. We should firmly believe that in this battle Allah did not leave the Muslims to themselves, because they were very few in number and resources, and just as the words of the Qur'an indicate, in this manner the angels took part in this battle.

Imam Bukhari, in the chapter "Thuhud al-Mala'ikah Badr" (The Presence of the Angels at Badr), says: from Ibn Ishaq, from Jarir, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Mu'adh ibn Rifa'ah ibn Rafi' al-Zurqi, from his father (and he was among the people of Badr), that Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "What do you consider about the people of Badr?" He replied: "We consider them to be the best of the Muslims." Jibril said: "Likewise, we consider those among the angels who were at Badr to be the best of the angels." (Bukhari)

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verse 10:

When the Muslims were humbly supplicating at the court of Allah, Allah answered them that He was sending down a thousand angels to help them, who would descend continuously. This announcement shows that the matter was very great, and that in Allah's sight the establishment of the religion (iqamat al-din) was of great importance. Yet Allah, the Exalted, repeatedly makes clear here that in this world the means (asbab) do not have such importance that deviation from them is impossible. The real authority lies with the will (mashi'ah) of Allah. Therefore, regarding means, the believer should keep his mind clear. The acceptance of Allah's help, and then its announcement, was merely a glad tiding through which the believers were to be reassured. As for victory, it was from Allah.

This is the reality which the Qur'an here wants to fix in the minds of the believers, so that they do not place complete reliance on means.

It was the duty of the Muslims to throw their entire strength into this battle and keep nothing in reserve. They were to overcome the wavering that had arisen among some of them at the outset, because at that time they were truly facing a real and concrete danger. Carrying out the command of Allah, they were to advance and keep their trust in the help of Allah. That alone was sufficient for them, so that they might perform their part of the role well. After that comes the work of Divine power, and Divine power itself manages its affairs. Whatever measures were taken and whatever information was given beyond this was merely for the reassurance of the Muslims, to steady their feet, because they were facing a real danger. For the community of Muslims it was sufficient to be assured that the armies of Allah were with them and that victory was destined for them, for victory comes from Allah, and Allah is with them. He is the Mighty, He is the Victorious, He is the Wise, and He places every matter in its true place.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verse 11:

This episode of drowsiness is also extraordinary and astonishing. It was a psychological state that overcame the Muslims before the battle. It was purely the work of Divine command, Allah's special planning and decree. When the two armies came face to face, a degree of fear overtook the Muslims, because they had not expected that so great a host would come forth. For this reason they were also not prepared, and suddenly drowsiness overtook them.

When this drowsiness departed, they were completely refreshed and invigorated. Their hearts were filled with tranquillity. These circumstances had overtaken them at Uhud as well. People became restless, and Allah cast drowsiness upon them, and they were reassured. I used to pass over these verses after reading them and would think that this was an event of the distant past. I would read this account in the Qur'an and think that only Allah, who informed us of it, knows its secret. But when difficulties came upon me, and some moments of great constriction and distress passed over me, then I understood the meaning of these verses. Once I was seized by an unknown fear; it was the time of sunset, and suddenly for a few minutes drowsiness came upon me, and when this state passed I felt that I was not the same person I had been before that drowsiness. My self was extremely calm. My heart was at peace and I was immersed in deep tranquillity. How this process was completed in a few moments, how this sudden transformation took place, I do not know. But what did happen is that the account of Badr and Uhud became clear to my understanding. After that experience I grasped this account with my whole being, not merely intellectually; it became a living reality within my existence. It was not merely imagination or thought. I clearly saw that the hand of Divine Power was at work in it, and in a very subtle way, tranquillity was bestowed upon me.

On the day of Badr, this drowsiness was an unseen divine aid for the community of Muslims. "Idh yughashikumu al-nu'as amanatan": Remember when your Lord caused drowsiness to overtake you as a form of security from Him, bestowing upon you a state of peace and fearlessness. In this verse the words yughashikumu al-nu'as and amanatan all cast a delicate and transparent light upon this atmosphere and sketch the general scene of that time. From them it becomes clear what the days and nights of the Muslims were at that time, and what the difference was between their general condition and their psychological state.

Now observe the account of the rain.

"Wa yunazzilu 'alaykum min al-sama'i ma'an liyutahhirakum bihi wa yudhhiba 'ankum rijza al-shaytani wa liyarbita 'ala qulubikum wa yuthabbita bihi al-aqdam" (8:11): And He was sending down upon you water from the sky, so that He might purify you by it, remove from you the defilement of Satan, strengthen your hearts, and make your feet firm by it.

This event occurred shortly before the battle, and this too was a special kind of aid for the community of the Muslims.

Ali ibn Talha narrated from Hadrat Ibn Abbas that on the day of Badr, the place where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) camped was such that between the polytheists and the water there was a sand dune, which was a stony place. On that day the Muslims were very exhausted. In such circumstances Satan began to whisper into their hearts: you claim that you are the friends of Allah and that the Messenger of Allah is among you, yet the polytheists have taken possession of the water, and your condition is that you pray while in a state of ritual impurity. Thereupon Allah sent down heavy rain. The Muslims drank water and also performed purification, and Allah purified them from the filth of Satan. When the rain fell, the sand also settled, and people and animals could walk upon it with ease. In this way they advanced. Allah aided the Prophet with a thousand angels; under the command of Jibril there were five hundred angels who were equipped with every kind of equipment, and under the command of Mikail there were also five hundred angels.

This situation arose at the time when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had not changed his camp on the advice of Hubab ibn Mundhir. He advised that it was appropriate for us to settle near the waters of Badr and, by making a basin of water, cut off the water of the opposing camp.

"It is well known that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out for Badr, he first camped at the water nearest to him. Then Hubab ibn Mundhir came forward and asked whether the place where he had been ordered to camp was from Allah; could they alter it, or was it a matter of military stratagem and planning? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said that he had chosen this place purely on the basis of military thinking. Upon this he said that this place was then not suitable for a military camp. It was appropriate that they lead them to the last water, which was close to the polytheists, and that they would hold back from the enemy all the water beyond that last water. They would drink themselves and give drink to their animals; thus they would have water and the enemy would not have water. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then ordered the army accordingly and acted upon this advice."

In the night before Hubab ibn al-Mundhir's advice, the Muslims were in the condition that Allah mentions as a favour to the community that took part in Badr. This aid that Allah provided was a second aid. It was both spiritual and material, because in deserts life depends upon water. Water is the means of victory, and in deserts an army without water is defeated in its mind. And spiritually, in that the Muslims emerged even from the whisperings of Satan. They were praying in a state of ritual impurity, and at that time they had not even been granted permission for tayammum. That permission was granted much later, in the battle of Banu al-Mustaliq, namely in the 5th year of the Hijra. In such circumstances Satan cast psychological whisperings and produced psychological and spiritual unease among the people, so that when these people entered that battle they would be troubled spiritually, and before the material defeat they would already have been defeated inwardly, and they would have been broken from within. In such circumstances this special aid of Allah came.

"Wa yunazzilu 'alaykum min al-sama'i ma'an liyutahhirakum bihi wa yudhhiba 'ankum rijza al-shaytani wa liyarbita 'ala qulubikum wa yuthabbita bihi al-aqdam" (8:11): And He was sending down upon you water from the sky, so that He might purify you by it, remove from you the defilement of Satan, strengthen your hearts, and make your feet firm by it.

Thus, alongside the material aid, the spiritual aid is also fully accomplished. Through the water the hearts were reassured, and through the purity of the soul they were refreshed. Because of the rain the sand settled and their steps also became firm.

Beyond these measures, Allah gave special instructions to the angels: that they should make firm the feet of the believers and cast fear into the hearts of the disbelievers, and the angels were commanded to take an actual part in the battle.

This is a great matter. In this battle, Allah Himself is present along with the host of angels, and the angels are coming to help the believers. It is so great a matter that it can by no means be overlooked. Think! How did the angels take part? How many people did they kill? In what manner did they kill them? This is a great matter, and of very great importance. In the group that undertakes the establishment of the religion (iqamat-e-din), the angels take part alongside it, and the angels share in its work.

Our belief is that among the creatures of the Lord of the worlds there is a creature called the angels (malaika), but what their nature and essence are, we have been given only as much knowledge as Allah has told us. Therefore we also do not know the manner in which this creature rendered help to the believers. The Qur'an says that the Lord, exalted is He, commanded them to be a source of steadfastness for the believers, and that "I am with you," and they did this work, because they are a creature bound to the command of Allah. But we do not know how they did this work. Allah also commanded that you strike the necks of the disbelievers and strike every one of their joints, so that they are no longer able to function, and they did so. But how did they do it? We do not know this. We have knowledge of them only to the extent that Allah has told us. Then Allah's command was that terror be cast into the hearts of the disbelievers, and it was cast, and it was done. Because Allah's promise is true. But we also do not know the modalities of this, because these disbelievers are creatures of Allah, and He knows best about His creation, how it will affect them. He comes between a person and his heart, and He is nearer to him than his jugular vein.

To discuss the modalities of these actions is contrary to the temperament of the religion of Islam, and this manner of conduct does not suit the seriousness of this religion. The temperament of Islam is that it is a practical religion, and it keeps belief, ideas and concepts also within the practical sphere. But in later periods, these discussions became more prominent in the scholastic theology (ilm al-kalam) of the Muslims, and this happened when people became free from the positive and practical work of Islam, and the scholarly and cultural colour came to dominate them. But the real matter was that if Muslims were on the battlefield, with the angels engaged in combat alongside them, and Allah were with the angels and the Muslims, then this practical situation would be more beneficial for Muslims than that cultural wrangling and debate.

This is the conclusion of that discourse and of the revelation of this great and dreadful reality. It is stated here what the background of that battle was, and due to which realities some were granted victory and for others defeat came to pass. That great background was:

"Dhalika bi-annahum shaqqu Allah wa Rasulahu, wa man yushaqiq Allah wa Rasulahu fa-inna Allah shadid al-iqab" — "This is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger, and whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, indeed Allah is severe in punishment."

This was not an event that occurred suddenly, nor was it an accidental incident that happened and passed away. Allah granted victory to the community of Muslims, made it dominant over its enemies, and placed awe in the hearts of its enemies. Armed angels came to their aid. This was because those people had opposed Allah and His Messenger. They chose for themselves a front which was not the front of Allah, and they went into the ranks opposed to Allah and His Messenger. They began hostility against God and His Messenger, and they had become an obstacle to the establishment of the Islamic system of life.

"Wa man yushaqiq Allah wa Rasulahu fa-inna Allah shadid al-iqab": "And whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, indeed Allah is severe in punishment." That is, Allah sends severe punishment upon such people. Allah is so powerful that He can send punishment upon them, and they are so weak that they do not have the capacity to bear that punishment.

This is the continuous Sunnah (established practice) of Allah, and it is His principle. It is not something sudden, a mishap, or a coincidence. It is the continuous Sunnah of Allah that on this earth, whenever a community arises with the purpose that it will establish the sovereignty of Allah here, and only the Islamic system of life will be established here, and some enemy of Allah rises up against that community and begins hostility with that community, and such people also possess power, force and influence, then Allah's help is with that community, provided that this community moves steadfastly towards its goal, remains content in the way of the Lord, relies upon Him, and its journey on its path continues.

In the closing part of this scene, those who have opened hostility against Allah and His Messenger are addressed. The awe and then the defeat you have suffered in this world are not the end of the matter, because this religion, its establishment and its community are not a affair confined to this brief span of worldly life. The matter extends far beyond this world and this universe. It has consequences in the life after this life, and they are these: ﴿This is your punishment; so taste it. And indeed, for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire.﴾ This will be the real outcome, and this punishment will be of a very different kind and greater than the punishment inflicted on you when you were terrified and when blows fell on your necks and joints.

----

After describing the events and circumstances of the Battle of Badr, and after showing that the hand of divine power was at work behind them, and that Allah's support and help were involved in them, and after understanding that the Muslims in all that striving were a veil for the hand of divine power: it was Allah who brought the Messenger out of his home. They did not set out merely to display strength, nor to commit oppression. It was Allah who decided which of the two groups would fall into the hands of the Muslims, and it was He who cut off the roots of the criminals, so that truth might become truth and falsehood might become falsehood, even though the criminals disliked this. It was Allah who sent to their aid the angels who came in succession. Then it was Allah who caused drowsiness to overcome them, and sent down water upon them from the heavens to purify them, to rid them of the filth of Satan, to strengthen their hearts and to make their footing firm. And it was Allah who commanded the angels to make the feet of the Muslims firm and to cast terror into the hearts of the disbelievers. It was Allah who made the angels partners in that battle, and commanded them: strike above the necks and strike every finger-tip of them. Then it was Allah who gave them spoils of war, although when they left their homes they had neither wealth nor equipment.

Now that the preceding events have been related, this truth is restated so that it remains fixed in their minds: that a decisive battle does not depend merely on equipment, provisions and resources, but that the help of God, His planning and His will play the decisive role in it. In this path, the real equipment is reliance upon God (tawakkul ʿalallah). Supplication to God, entreaty and weeping before Him, and God's planning and decree are decisive in it.

This scene is still firmly lodged in the minds of those people. Such circumstances and such an atmosphere are most suitable for this lesson, and in such an atmosphere advice is accepted. Accordingly, in such an atmosphere the Muslims are given this counsel: the demand of their faith is that, when they stand against the disbelievers, they display steadfastness and never accept flight or defeat. Especially since victory and defeat lie in the hands of God, and you believe in this. The decision of victory and defeat is not made only by apparent causes, especially when God Himself has taken the planning and command of a battle into His own hands. Just as He is the one who plans all affairs, and it is He who causes the disbelievers to be killed at the hands of the believers, it is He who places your arrow on the target. The believers are merely a veil and a pretext for the hand of divine power, and through this pretext God grants them the reward of jihad, and casts terror into the disbelievers on account of the Muslims. He loosens the fabric of their planning and afflicts them with punishment in this world and the Hereafter, because in truth they are waging hostility against God and His Messenger.

﴿O you who have believed, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing [in order of battle], do not turn your backs to them.﴾

The harsh manner of speech the Qur'an has adopted in this matter, and the severe punishment it has prescribed, and its ruling that whoever flees in defeat shall deserve the wrath of God and his abode shall be Hell, are all a warning.

O you who have believed, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing [in order of battle], do not turn your backs to them. Whoever turns his back to them on such an occasion, unless it is a stratagem of war or to join another company, he will incur the wrath of God, his abode will be Hell, and it is a wretched destination.

The meaning of this is: when you are in a state of "zahf", that is, when a face-to-face confrontation in battle occurs, do not take flight at that time, unless this flight is in the form of a war stratagem, so that you are fleeing for the sake of a better position, or flight is ordered for the sake of some other excellent plan; or you are fleeing in order to join another military company; or you are retreating to the military headquarters in order to attack again. If, outside these circumstances, you turn your backs to the enemy, you will become deserving of punishment, you will incur the wrath of God, and your abode will be Hell.

Some reports have stated that this command applied only to the people of Badr, or to those expeditions in which the Holy Prophet ﷺ himself took part. But the majority of scholars and exegetes hold that this verse and command are general, and that fleeing from a face-to-face confrontation is one of the seven major sins concerning which the Prophet ﷺ used the word "mubiqat". Bukhari and Muslim have related the narration of Abu Hurairah that the Prophet said: "Avoid the seven destructive sins." It was said: "O Messenger of God, what are they?" He said: "Associating partners with God, sorcery, killing a person whose killing is forbidden, consuming usury, consuming the property of an orphan, turning one's back in a face-to-face battle, and falsely accusing chaste, unaware believing women."

Imam Abu Bakr al-Jassas has given details about this in Ahkam al-Quran, and it will be useful to reflect upon them here. "The Almighty says: 'And whoever turns his back to them on that day, unless it is a stratagem of war or to join another company...'" Abu Nadrah related from Abu Saʿid that this concerned the matter of the Day of Badr, because on that day, to whom would they have fled? The only option was that they would have joined the polytheists, since there were no Muslims other than themselves. And the Prophet had not commanded everyone to set out, nor was it their opinion that a battle should take place. All thought that the encounter would be with the caravan only. The Prophet set out with a slight force. Therefore Abu Nadrah's statement that on that day there were no Muslims other than these people, and that if they had fled they would have fled only to the disbelievers, is incorrect, and the proof is what we have explained. Some people say that on the day of the Battle of Badr, it was not permissible for them to flee and turn their backs, because on that day the Prophet ﷺ was among them, and it was not permissible to abandon the Prophet. The Almighty says: "It was not for the people of Medina and the Bedouins around them to remain behind the Messenger of God, nor to prefer their own selves over his self." So it was not permissible for them to thwart their Prophet and abandon him to the enemy. Although God was his guarantor and their helper, He had taken responsibility to protect him from the disbelievers, as it was said: "And God will protect you from the people." Therefore it was obligatory upon them to help the Prophet, whether the enemy was many or few. And the argument of these people is also that on that day the Prophet alone was a unit, and turning one's back in battle was permissible only on condition that one fled toward another company of the mujahidin. On that day the Prophet was the only group; no other group was stationed anywhere apart from the people of Badr. Ibn Umar says: I was in an army. People attacked suddenly and we returned to Medina. We said: we are among those who flee. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I am your fi'ah (a body to fall back upon)." Therefore, if a person is far from the Prophet and returns, his returning to the Prophet is permissible. And if the Prophet is present in the battle, then there will be no other group with which soldiers may flee to join. "And whoever turns his back to them on that day..." Concerning this verse, Ibn al-Hasan says that the people of Badr were subjected to very strict commands, and this verse: "Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met, it was only Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned." Those who fled on the day when the two armies met were made to slip by Satan because of some of their evil deeds. This is because these people fled from the Prophet. Also, in the Battle of Hunayn these people fled, leaving the Prophet ﷺ. Therefore God punished them for that act.

"And [recall] the day of Hunayn, when your large numbers pleased you, but they did not avail you at all, and the earth was confining for you in spite of its vastness, and you turned back fleeing." This was the ruling for the situation when the Prophet was with them, whether the enemy was few or many, because God gave no concession in it. In another verse God says: "O Prophet, urge the believers to fight. If there are among you twenty steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you one hundred, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve." This command was for the time when the Prophet ﷺ was not with them, and God knows best. In such circumstances, the earlier ruling was that twenty would confront two hundred and not flee the field, and if the enemy exceeded that number, then retreating for the sake of a good tactic in attack would be permissible. But this ruling was later abrogated, and another verse was revealed: "Now God has lightened your burden, and He knows that there is weakness in you. So if there are among you one hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand by the permission of God."

It is reported from Ibn Abbas that the original obligation was that one man should not flee from ten. Then it was reduced and it was said: "Now God has lightened your burden and known that there is weakness in you." Now the obligation became that one should not flee from one to two hundred. Ibn Abbas says that now the ruling is: if one person flees from two, it is flight; but if one flees before three, it is not flight. The shaykh says that the flight meant here is the flight intended in this verse. The verse has stipulated that one man should stand firm against two, and if the number is more than two, then it is permissible for a mujahid to flee with the intention of regrouping for renewed battle and joining the army. But if an individual flees to a non-Muslim group that is not one of the Muslims, he too will deserve the threat contained in this verse, because the verse commands: "And whoever turns his back to them on that day, unless it is a stratagem of war or to join another company, then he has incurred wrath from God." This is why the Prophet ﷺ said that he is a second company (fi'ah) for every Muslim. When Umar ibn al-Khattab learned that Abu Ubayd ibn Masud had fought with an army and was martyred but had not fled, he said: "May God have mercy on Abu Ubayd; if he had returned to me, I would have been a second company for him." And when Abu Ubayd's companions returned, Umar said: "I am a second company for you." He did not impose any severity upon them nor call them to account. The same ruling holds with us (that is, according to the Hanafis: until the Muslim army reaches 21,000, because it is not permissible for a force of 21,000 to retreat from its position. If their number is doubled, unless they do so as a battle stratagem, which means moving from one trench to another, or adopting some other tactic in which there is no element of fleeing from battle, or joining another army and units). Muhammad ibn al-Hasan has related that if the army reaches 21,000, it is obligatory upon it to confront the enemy in every case. There is no difference of opinion among the Hanafis on this. The Hanafis have argued from the hadith of al-Zuhri, which he related from Ubaydullah ibn Abdullah, that Ibn Abbas related from the Prophet: he said: "The best companions are four, the best military units are four hundred, the best armies are four thousand, and an army of 21,000 will not be considered small, nor will it be overcome." Some narrations have these words: "If any people among you numbers 21,000, it will not be overcome, provided there is unity among them." Imam al-Tahawi has related that Imam Malik was asked: "Is it permissible for us to refrain from jihad and fighting against a person who does not follow the commands of God and judges by other than God's law?" He said: "If there are 21,000 people like you present, then retreat is forbidden. And if there are not that many, you have leeway not to fight." And this questioner was Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz; Ibn Abdullah was the son of Umar. And this statement is in accordance with the opinion reported from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. The narration from the Prophet ﷺ concerning 12,000 is the root and principle on this subject. Even if the number of the disbelievers is very large, it is not permissible for the Muslims to flee. Even if they are many times more, because the condition the Prophet laid down, "if there is unity among them," thereby made unity obligatory upon them.

In the same way, Ibn al-Arabi has also given these details in his book Ahkam al-Quran. Regarding this ruling he said: there is a difference of opinion as to whether the prohibition of fleeing from the battlefield was specific to the Day of Badr, or whether this ruling continues until the Day of Resurrection.

It is reported from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri that this prohibition was specific to the Day of Badr, because the second company for that day was only the Messenger of God himself. This is also the opinion of Nafi, Hasan, Qatadah, Yazid, Ibn Habib and al-Dahhak.

It is reported from Ibn Abbas and all other scholars that this ruling remains until the Day of Resurrection. Those who restricted it to the Day of Badr relied on "And whoever turns his back to them on that day," claiming that "that day" refers to Badr, whereas "that day" (yawmaʾidh) refers to the day of the battle (yawm al-zahf), that is, the day of battle in general.

The proof is that these verses were revealed after the fighting at Badr, and by the time they were revealed the Battle of Badr had ended. What was to happen on that day had already happened. And it is established from the Prophet ﷺ, as we have already related a hadith earlier, that the major sins include this; and among them is counted fleeing on the day of battle. This is an explicit text on the issue, after which disagreement should be dispelled. We have also pointed out the matter that caused some people to suppose that it refers to the Day of Badr.

Our view is that the opinion which Ibn al-'Arabi related from all the scholars, and which is also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, is the one we too adopt. This is because fleeing from the ranks in battle is an extremely evil act, and it has far-reaching consequences, both from the standpoint of the movement and from the standpoint of belief and ideology.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verse 16:

The heart and mind of the believer must be extremely firm, such that it does not waver before any power of the earth, and its connection must be with a power that has complete control over its affairs and complete dominion over the servants. When the heart and mind of a believer wavers upon seeing dangers, this wavering should not result in flight, because death is in the hands of Allah. Therefore it is not permissible for a believer to turn his back out of fear of death. This command is not such that one is commanded beyond one's capacity, because the believer is a human being and his enemy is also a human being. In this respect they stand, as it were, on the same level. Then the distinctive feature of the believer is that his connection is with a power over which no one prevails. If he is alive, then he is the servant of Allah and is turned towards Him; and if he dies, he too returns to Allah. If martyrdom has been decreed for him, then his position is still far better than that of his enemy, because the enemy confronts Allah and His Messenger. This is why a definite command is given:

﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day, unless he is maneuvering for battle or joining another company, he has certainly incurred anger from Allah, and his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾

...Here the style of speech that the Qur'an has adopted contains many indications. ﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾ and ﴿whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾. This is in fact a physical expression of defeat and rout, and a most contemptuous picture is given of those who flee. And the impression is given that one should show one's face to the enemy, not one's back. Then ﴿he has certainly incurred anger from Allah﴾: it is as if the one who suffers defeat in fact turns his back, and with it comes the wrath of Allah, and this wrath of Allah takes him to Hell, which is an evil abode. ﴿And his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ Thus, in the manner of expression too, the scene of turning one's back on the day of battle is depicted in such a way that the ugliness and repugnance of this act become clearly apparent, and no person of honor approves of it.

After the prohibition of turning one's back on the day of battle, the context now tells the truth that behind this encounter the hand of divine power is in fact at work. It is Allah who killed your enemies; it is He who guides your arrow to the right target. And the reward you are given is only so that the believers succeeded in this trial, struggled, and Allah made them deserving of this reward and granted them recompense.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verse 17:

It is related in the narrations that the "striking" mentioned here refers to this: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took pebbles and sand in his hand and threw them toward the army of the disbelievers, and at that moment he said: "Shahat al-wujuh, shahat al-wujuh" (May their faces be disfigured, may their faces be disfigured), meaning, may they become ugly and repulsive. And the pebbles and sand, by this verse, fell upon those faces whose killing in this battle had been decreed.

However, the meaning of this verse is general. The purpose is that, although outwardly it was the Prophet (ﷺ) and the army of Islam who were acting, behind all of it the hand of divine power was at work. This is also why the sentence that follows in the verse is: ﴿وَلِيُبْلِيَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ مِنْهُ بَلَاءً حَسَنًا﴾ ("and that He might test the believers with a good test from Him"), meaning, so that He might give the believers this opportunity of trial and, by passing through it successfully, they might become deserving of reward, although the victory had already been decreed by Him. Thus this success was a cause of further reward in every condition, both before and after. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing"). Surely Allah is Hearing and Knowing; He was hearing your supplications and was well aware of your circumstances.

Such was the whole matter: Allah made it a path for you to demonstrate His power. But He made it so only when you had shown sincerity. That is why He granted you victory and you also became deserving of reward. Allah always does just as He did at Badr.

﴿That is so, and surely Allah weakens the plots of the disbelievers.﴾ This is the matter concerning you, and the matter concerning the disbelievers is that Allah is the one who weakens their schemes.

This is Allah's second support. Allah's arrangement does not end with His killing your enemies by His own hand, and His guiding your arrows to their exact targets, and His providing you with a fine field of trial so that He may give you reward. He also does this: whatever plots the disbelievers devise, He keeps loosening their bonds and weakens their stratagems. Therefore you should not fear, and in this battle the defeat of the believers simply does not arise as a question, nor does the question of the Muslims turning their backs arise.

Thus, from these phrases, the answer to all questions comes forth of its own accord. If Allah Himself kills the disbelievers, and if Allah Himself is the one who strikes with arrows or stones, and He Himself is the one who arranges this field of trial in order to reward the Muslims, and if He Himself is the one who weakens the plots of the enemies, then the question of dispute concerning the spoils (al-anfal) and the wealth of booty does not even arise, because the authority over affairs also lies in Allah's hand, and both the beginning and the end are in accordance with His arrangement. As for human beings and Muslims, they are merely the signs and indications of the divine decree.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 8, verse 19:

When the discussion reached the point where "Allah is the One who weakens the schemes of the disbelievers," the address turns toward the disbelievers. These are the very people who, before that battle, sought a decision and raised their hands in supplication before Allah, saying: "O Allah, of the two opposing parties, make war against the one that is misguided. Destroy whoever speaks things that are not known as good (ma'ruf), and destroy whoever goes against the ties of kinship." This supplication was made by Abu Jahl. So Allah decided the battle against them, and now they are addressed and mocked: "It was you who used to pray for a curse." The point is that what happened at Badr occurred in accordance with Allah's enduring practice (sunnat jariyah), and that the numerical strength and assembly of the disbelievers did not benefit them, because they could not alter Allah's enduring practice, and Allah was with the believers.

...

إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ ...

You used to pray for a decision, saying: whichever of the Muslims and the polytheists is upon the truth, let Allah decide the battle in his favour, or let it go against whichever of the two parties is misguided and takes a position against the ties of kinship. Allah accepted this supplication. He turned the battle against you. Thereby your claim was confirmed, and the battle was decided against the more misguided party. If you truly wished to identify the misguided party, the party opposed to brotherhood, then you have come to know which party it is. Therefore your duty is to observe the outcome of the battle, come to Islam, abandon shirk and disbelief, and give up your hostile attitude towards the Muslims and the Messenger of Allah.

إِنْ تَسْتَفْتِحُوا فَقَدْ جَاءَكُمُ الْفَتْحُ ۚ وَإِنْ تَنْتَهُوا فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ (Say to these disbelievers:) If you sought a decision, then take it: the decision has come before you. Now desist, it is better for you.

And after it comes a warning: وَإِنْ تَعُودُوا نَعُدْ (But if you return to this folly, We too will return to the same punishment).

The outcome is known to all. In a contest between truth and falsehood, the multitude of armies is not decisive, nor can outcomes be changed in that manner. وَلَنْ تُغْنِيَ عَنْكُمْ فِئَتُكُمْ شَيْئًا وَلَوْ كَثُرَتْ (Your company, however large it may be, will not avail you anything at all.)

If Allah is on the side of the Muslims, the multitude of the disbelievers can do nothing, and here the situation is: وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ (and that Allah is with the believers).

Because in a battle of this kind there is no balance between the forces of the two sides. Allah is with the believers, standing in their line, while the disbelievers have only men like themselves, who stand in the second line. The outcome of a battle between such parties is known in advance.

The polytheists of Arabia also acknowledged this reality. Their conception and knowledge of Allah was not as superficial or as complex as the superficial views that disbelievers later adopted about Allah. For the shirk of the Arabs was not of the kind that would outright deny the Divine Being, nor were they utterly ignorant of the truth. Their shirk consisted only in not restricting worship and servitude to Allah alone, in not taking guidance and laws solely from Allah. Even this degree of shirk did not, in fact, fit well with their recognition of divinity.

Earlier we have related in the accounts of this battle that Khafaf ibn Ima ibn Rahdah al-Ghifari, or his father Ima ibn Rahdah al-Ghifari, sent livestock with his son to the army of Quraysh as a gift, and also offered them weapons and young men if they wished. The Quraysh answered through his son: "You have fulfilled the right of kinship and discharged your obligation. By God, if our war were with humans, we are not so weak; and if our war were with God, as Muhammad supposes, then no human can fight against God."

A similar statement is found in the books of biography concerning Akhnas ibn Shariq. He said to the Banu Zuhrah, and both were polytheists at that time: "O Banu Zuhrah, Allah has saved your wealth, and your companion Makhramah ibn Nawfal has returned safely." And a supplication of Abu Jahl (whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called the Pharaoh of this Ummah) is recorded in the books of biography: "O Allah, whichever of us is opposed to the ties of kinship and speaks things that are not known as good, then destroy him tomorrow."

Likewise is the saying of Hakim ibn Hizam, when the message of Utbah ibn Rabi'ah came to him that they should return from this battle. He said: "By God, that cannot be. We will not return until Allah decides between us and Muhammad."

This conception of the Divine Being was present with them, and they kept this reality in view on every occasion. It was not that they were atheists who neither knew nor accepted God, or who did not think that no one could fight against Allah, or who did not think that Allah is the one who decides between the parties and that no one can reject His command. The origin of their shirk lay in this: they did not take their guidance concerning the system of life from Allah alone, but also took it from others, although, as we have explained, they acknowledged the Divine Being. And this is the matter in which the Muslims of today and the polytheists of that time are alike. Yet the Muslims of today suppose that they are upon the religion of Muhammad, whereas the polytheists of Makkah at that time held this belief and claimed that they were upon the religion of their father Abraham. And this is why Abu Jahl, despite being Abu Jahl, was seeking a decision from Allah: "O Allah, whichever of us is most opposed to the ties of kinship, and whose speech is most against what is known as good, destroy him tomorrow." Such were his words.

As for the idols, of whom it is well known that they worshipped them, their belief about them was that they too were gods in the same way that Allah is God. The Qur'an has made clear their notions about God and has explained why they worshipped these idols. Allah the Exalted says: وَالَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا مِنْ دُونِهِ أَوْلِيَاءَ مَا نَعْبُدُهُمْ إِلَّا لِيُقَرِّبُونَا إِلَى اللَّهِ زُلْفَى (Those who take protectors other than Him say: "We worship them only so that they may bring us near to Allah in nearness.") This was their conception of divinity, namely that these deities were their intercessors. Viewed from this aspect, their real shirk was that they considered their deities to be intercessors before Allah's court. And their Islam would not have consisted merely in rejecting these intercessors; otherwise those who were called Hunafa, and who did not worship idols, would have been regarded as Muslims, but this is not the case. For the reality of Islam is that in belief and in action Allah alone is regarded as the sovereign, and those who do not regard Allah alone as the sovereign and the one to be obeyed are in shirk, whatever time and place they may be in. Their belief that there is no god but Allah cannot save them from this shirk, namely a merely doctrinal conception; nor can the mere fact that they perform the rites of servitude solely before Allah save them from shirk, for to that extent alone today's Muslims may be called Hunafa. Muslims become Muslims only when they can join together all the links and rings of Islam. That is, they must, along with regarding Allah as one, worshipping Him, and regarding Him as God, also affirm His sovereignty. They must accept His commands, His laws, and the values He has prescribed. This alone is real Islam, and this Islam is expressed in the testimony of faith: La ilaha illallah Muhammad rasulullah. This is the meaning of the testimony, and this meaning is recognised and accepted in Islamic belief and in the Islamic society. After this it is also necessary that those who affirm the testimony of faith in this sense be organised and active in a collective form, that they have their own Muslim leadership, and that they emerge from all Jahili defilements in the manner in which hair emerges cleanly from butter.

Those who truly wish to become Muslims should keep this reality in mind. They should not be deceived into thinking that they have become Muslims merely through belief or merely through the rites of servitude. Merely through these things people do not become true Muslims, unless they regard Allah alone as their sovereign and acknowledge no other person's sovereignty, and until they withdraw all their sympathies and friendships from Jahili societies.

This misunderstanding afflicts many sincere and righteous Muslims. In truth such sincere people do desire Islam, but they are caught in deception. Therefore it is the duty of such sincere Muslims first to remove the misunderstanding from minds concerning the nature of Islam, and to understand that those whom they call the polytheists of Arabia were not different from them in belief and practice: they acknowledged the Divine Being, and as we have said above, they regarded their idols as intercessors with Allah. Their real shirk was shirk in sovereignty, not in belief.

When it is necessary for ordinary sincere Muslims to understand this reality of Islam well, then those who undertake the work of establishing the religion and who seek to revive in the real world the Islamic system of life and the sovereignty of Allah have an even greater duty to understand this reality very clearly and in its depth. They should not speak about it in a vague manner, nor equivocate. They should tell people plainly and clearly that true Islam is this. This is the starting point of their work. If any movement deviates from this even slightly, it will go astray and begin to build upon wrong foundations, even though its members may be sincere and the movement itself may be engaged in great striving.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verses 20–23:

Commentary on verses 20 to 23: The address now turns back to the believers, and they are addressed continuously with "Yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū" (O you who believe). This address comes after the preceding themes, that Allah is with them, and in this address they are given the advice that they should obey Allah and His Messenger. They are warned against defiance towards Allah and the Messenger, and they should not be like those who hear the verses of Allah and behave as though they had not heard them. These people are deaf and dumb, even though they have eyes, ears and tongues. These people are the worst of beasts, because they hear like animals but do not find the path of guidance.

This call is addressed to those who have believed. They have been told to obey Allah and the Messenger of Allah, and not to turn away while hearing the verses and words of Allah. This call comes after the indications that had to precede it as a preface and introduction. Before this, the major events of this battle had been described: seeing the Divine Being, the concept of His planning, the assurance of His help and support, and the explicit statement that Allah is with the believers and that He weakens all the plans of the disbelievers. Therefore, after these, there is no option left except listening and obeying. Despite these realities, turning away from Allah and His Messenger appears to be an extremely ugly and reprehensible act. No intelligent person can commit such an act. This is why animals are also mentioned here, because the word (dawāb) includes humans in its natural sense. But the word dawāb is used more for livestock than for humans. Therefore, by applying this word to some humans, the concept of animals comes to mind automatically, and concerning those who are deaf and dumb and do not possess knowledge, the concept of animality is given. In effect, the ignorant are in reality animals, indeed worse than animals. Animals have ears, but they can only hear a few vague sounds. They also have a tongue, but they cannot speak words that convey meanings. Yes, animals have been given natural capacities, and they carry on the business of their lives according to that natural capacity, whereas human beings, even in determining the necessities of their lives, rely on their own intellect.

O you who believe, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you are hearing. And do not be like those who said, "We have heard," while they were not hearing. Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and dumb who do not use reason.

And why are these people the worst of beasts?

If Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And even if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being averse. Allah knows that there is no good in them, and if there were good in them, Allah would have granted them the ability to hear and accept. But because of their evil deeds they have destroyed their natural capacity. Since they had closed the doors of their minds and hearts, Allah too deprived them of the grace of hearing. Even if Allah were to make them understand, their attitude has become such that they would not accept it.

And even if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being averse (despite the absence of goodness). If He had made them hear, they would have turned away with indifference. Often it happens that the intellect grasps a matter, but the hearts have become so hardened that they do not accept it. Even if Allah makes them understand only to the extent of comprehension, they still remain deprived of acceptance. In the world there are countless people whose intellect is satisfied with the truth, but their hearts do not accept it.
