Following the brief survey of the events of Badr, the context now shifts to the statement of a general rule; this event and this scene are a particular instance of that rule. That seizing the disbelievers in a manner of extreme humiliation is a continuing and ongoing sunnah (established way of Allah), and it never undergoes any change. This treatment has continued since the time Allah set the struggle between truth and falsehood in motion in this world.

It is not Allah's sunnah to leave people to the waves of the sea, or to hand them over to the chances of time, so that they are bound by no principle or rule. Rather, Allah has bound all creation to His system of qadar and qada' (divine decree and destiny). The circumstances that the polytheists faced on the Day of Badr, or the circumstances they will face in future, are in accordance with Allah and His system of qada' and qadar. And in accordance with this same system, what happened to Pharaoh and the disbelievers before him also occurred.

"They rejected the signs of Allah, and Allah seized them for their sins," and they could not offer any defence against Allah's seizing, nor could they escape that punishment, because "Indeed, Allah is strong and severe in punishment."

Allah showered blessings upon those people. Through His grace and favour He gave them much, established their dominion over the earth, and they became heirs to that dominion. But Allah gives all such things to whomever He gives them as a test. He observes whether these people are thankful or ungrateful. The result, however, was that they did not show gratitude but rather displayed ingratitude, and beyond that they adopted a attitude of rebellion and insolence. Because of these blessings and powers they became tyrants and oppressors, and, sunk in wickedness and depravity, they gave themselves the form of a satanic force. When Allah's signs and miracles came to them, they adopted a posture of disbelief. Therefore, they became deserving that they be seized under the law which is the continuing sunnah for this universe: that when Allah's signs reach someone and people deny them, Allah seizes them and brings them to account and lays them bare.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verses 53–54:

Allah destroyed them only when they denied the signs of Allah. Before that, He did not take any action against them, even though they were disbelievers. This is the established way (sunnat jariyah) of Allah, and it is an act of His grace that He has set this principle. And ﴿We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾. The Pharaoh's people, and those nations before them to whom the signs of Allah were sent, denied them, and Allah sent destruction and ruin upon them. Why was this action taken against them? Because they were wrongdoers (ظالم). Here the word ẓulm is used in the sense of kufr or shirk, and in the Qur'an this word is often used in these meanings.

Here, this verse requires deep reflection:

"This is in accordance with the sunnah whereby Allah does not change a blessing which He has bestowed upon a people until they change what is in themselves."

This is an important aspect of Allah's justice toward His servants. When Allah gives any servant a blessing, He does not take it away until the servant himself changes his intention, changes his conduct, and changes his ways. And he does not make himself deserving of Allah taking away from him the blessing that was given to him. Because whatever is given to anyone here is given as a test and trial, and when servants do not value that bestowal and do not give thanks for it, Allah takes that bestowal back from them. And in this there is also an aspect of human dignity and honour: Allah has linked His system of decree (qaza wa qadar) and of giving and taking to the very conduct of the human being, and He runs His system of decree in such a way that a person is repaid according to how he walks and acts. The action a person adopts, the way his intention works, and the path, conduct and attitude they choose for themselves, the system of decree runs with them accordingly. A third aspect is that a great responsibility for his deeds is placed upon the human being, and with honour and dignity he is given the opportunity that, if he wishes, he may respond to Allah's favours and His grace with gratitude, and thereby have them increased, just as through ingratitude these favours are also withdrawn.

This is an important truth, and within the Islamic conception of man this truth is very significant. The question is: what is the place of the system of decree in this universe in relation to humanity? And what is the connection of the human being with the universe in which he lives? From this system of decree it becomes clear how great is the importance of the human being in the sight of Allah, and from this perspective how much honour Islam has bestowed upon man, in that man's own affairs and in the great upheavals that occur in this universe, the human attitude has been declared a decisive factor. Through his positive attitude come positive results, and through his negative attitude he meets negative and unpleasant results. Whereas today's materialistic conception of man is that he is a debased and worthless creature, bound by the compulsory laws of materialism. He is also helpless before economic forces. He is shown as a helpless being before the final laws of history, and he is shown as bound by compulsory rules of progress. In short, in the materialistic conception of the modern age, the compulsions it describes leave man with no standing or worth. Therefore he is given the notion that he is a helpless, debased and weak creature before these natural compulsions.

This truth gives the idea that there is a mutual relation between action and its consequence, and that in this universe man is an effective creature. Allah does not do any injustice to him. The sunnah of Allah and His natural laws run in accordance with His system of decree, in which there is no injustice to human beings.

Indeed Allah is not unjust to the servants. Thus Allah destroyed the people of Pharaoh also because of their deeds; He did not wrong them without cause. Once again, reflect on the verse:

"This is in accordance with the sunnah of Allah whereby He does not change a blessing which He has bestowed upon a people until that people change what is in themselves."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verse 55 (part 1 of 2):

Lesson No. 86 at a Glance

This is the fourth and final lesson of Surah al-Anfal. In it, certain rules are laid down concerning peace and war with other nations and blocs. Alongside this, the internal organization of the Islamic society and the nature of its relations with other organizations are regulated. The discussion covers the nature of treaties between Islam and other peoples in various circumstances. It also defines the Islamic viewpoint on blood, colour and race, regional affiliation, and leadership and ideologies.

This lesson also contains rulings on these subjects that are final on their topic, and some that were meant for the stage in which this surah was revealed, for specific conditions, or for a particular incident, and which were later amended and took their final form afterwards. That is, these rulings took their final form in Surah al-Tawbah. Surah al-Tawbah is among the last surahs of the Madinan period.

These rulings and principles include the following matters.

Those who make treaties with the Islamic bloc and then break their covenant are, on this earth, the worst of creatures. Therefore, it is among the duties of the Islamic bloc to give them an instructive discipline, and to teach them a lesson such that it becomes a good warning both for these people and for those who come after them, or for the powers that stand behind them.

If the Islamic government fears that a treaty partner nation will act treacherously, or will betray trust in the covenant, then the Islamic leadership has the right to place the covenant before them and announce that it no longer has any standing. After that, if the Islamic government punishes those people, it is free to do so, so that it may frighten those who are active against the Islamic government and are preparing to attack.

It is the duty of the Islamic bloc to keep its defensive forces alert at all times and to develop its military strength to the utmost possible extent, so that on this earth the rightly guided power is the great power, and all false powers tremble before it. All false powers in the earth should know of its strength and be fearful of it, and should not dare to attack. They should bow before the sovereignty of Allah, and the situation should become such that there is no obstacle anywhere in the world to a caller to Islam, and no obstacle before those who wish to accept the call of Islam, and no power should claim supreme political authority for itself, but rather the system of government should run only by Allah.

* If any of the non-Muslims wishes to make a treaty of peace with the Islamic camp, and does not become an obstacle in the way of the Islamic government, then it is the duty of the leadership of the Islamic government to accept it and conclude the treaty. If they intend some secret conspiracy, and no sign of deception is apparent, then it is their duty to leave their secret intentions to Allah. Allah is the One who protects from the evil of such deceivers.

* Jihad is obligatory upon the Muslims, even if the number of the enemy is double the number of the Muslims. By the grace of Allah, victory over their enemies will be granted to the Muslims. One of them can face twenty, and even in weak circumstances one of them can face two. Therefore, the obligation of jihad does not allow the waiting period for the moment when the number of believers and their enemy is equal. So the prepared strength of the Muslims is sufficient, and it is obligatory upon them to keep as much strength prepared as possible. They should rely upon Allah, remain steadfast in battle, be patient in difficulties, and leave the outcome to Allah, because He possesses spiritual strength besides material strength.

* The first target of the Islamic front should be that it shatters all the sources of tyrannical power. If they think that taking soldiers captive and then releasing them in exchange for a war ransom is not beneficial, then they should by no means do so, because it is not the work of the Messenger and the Muslims to let tyrannical powers survive after thoroughly shattering them, and to establish their supreme authority in the region. Crushing the enemy thoroughly is better than taking captives and extracting ransom before that.

* It has been made lawful for the Muslims to take spoils of war, and likewise it has been permitted for the Muslims to release prisoners and receive a war ransom, but only at the time when they have thoroughly broken the strength of the enemy, established their supreme authority, and their power and majesty have been firmly established.

* Disbelievers who are taken captive in the Islamic camp are told to take an interest in Islam, and to remember that if the spoils that were taken from you are returned, and you become Muslims, then Allah will give you something better than it. But if you commit treachery, then just as your end was in the Battle of Badr, the same will happen again.

* In Islamic society, gathering is based upon ideologies, and the bond of walayah (allegiance and friendship) is especially based upon ideology and the foundation of a shared movement. Therefore, those who believed and migrated, and those who gave shelter and support, these are in reality the walis (protectors and allies) of one another. As for those who accepted the ideology and also believed but did not migrate, there is no walayah between them and the believing emigrants. That is, the Abode of Islam is not bound to give them support, maintenance, and sympathy. Their support and sympathy by the Muslims is obligatory only when their creed and ideology are under attack, and they are being oppressed because of their beliefs and ideologies. However, there is one more condition in this matter as well, and it is that the oppression and aggression should not come from a people with whom the people of Islam have a treaty.

* Within the Islamic society too, the bond of friendship and sympathy exists only within the circle of those whose creed and ideology are of genuine faith, and who also have a shared movement for the Islamic revolution. But this does not mean that blood relatives (ulu al-arham) should not be considered deserving of preference over other people; rather, they should be considered closer. Provided that these relatives all adhere to the Islamic way of life and are working together for Islam. Mere kinship is not sufficient, meaning kinship in which there is no sharing of principles and beliefs and in which there is no movement toward a single purpose.

In brief, these are the main themes of this lesson, and these themes are the important subjects of the internal and external organization of the Islamic society. The details will be observed during the explanation of the verses.

Lesson No. 86: Explanation of Verses 55 to 75

Commentary on Verses 55 to 63:

These verses are a kind of practical guidance, at a time when the community of Muslims was practically confronting such circumstances. At that time the Islamic state was being founded in Madinah. In these practical circumstances, necessary commands were given to the Muslim community.

Most of these directives concern the law of nations (qanun bain al-mamalik) between the Islamic state of that time, or the fronts and states established around the Islamic government of that time. After these verses, the Holy Qur'an made some minor amendments to them, but these directives are the foundational directives of the Islamic law of nations.

These directives allow for the possibility that security treaties may be concluded between various international groups and states, provided that the parties to the treaty sincerely abide by its conditions. If any party is devising treachery and betrayal behind the cover of that treaty, and is preparing attacks and mischief, then the head of the Islamic state has the authority to openly cancel those treaties and inform the opposing party too, and then he has the authority to strike such traitors and betrayers at whatever time he wishes. This strike should be so severe and so instructive that no spiteful person, openly or secretly, should become an obstacle in any path against the Islamic state, or that they should not obstruct the arrival of the Islamic call to every person. Then the Islamic government has the authority to conclude a treaty with such people, and as long as no malicious intent appears from them, it should remain bound by the covenant with them.

This is a practical principle for the relations of neighbouring states within practical circumstances. This principle does not end mutual relations until the neighbouring states of the Islamic state place some material obstacle in the way of the spread of the Islamic call, and the reach of the preaching of Islam to people's ears is not stopped. But at the same time, this safeguard is also provided, that these treaties do not become a cause of conspiracies and plots against the enemy, and that behind these treaties these people do not intend a sudden and treacherous strike against the Islamic state.

What were the practical circumstances in which these directives were revealed? When the Muslim community migrated to Madinah, the situation that the Muslims faced there was summarized by Imam Ibn al-Qayyim in Zad al-Ma'ad as follows: "When the Prophet came to Madinah, there were three kinds of relations between him and the disbelievers. One kind of people were those who made reconciliation with the Prophet and promised that they would not oppose him, would not fight against him, would not take the side of his enemies, and would give aid, and that they would remain upon their disbelieving beliefs and remain peaceful. Their blood and property would be protected. The second kind were those who were his enemies and combatants. And the third kind were those who neither made a covenant nor fought against him, but kept waiting to see which way the camel would kneel. Among these people, some were those who sincerely desired his success, and some were those who desired the victory and triumph of his enemies. And some were those who outwardly joined the ranks of the Muslims but inwardly were with the enemies. These were the hypocrites. So the Prophet dealt with these people in the manner that the Lord, the Exalted, had commanded."

The people with whom he made a covenant of peace and who promised him were the three Jewish tribes living around Madinah: Banu Qaynuqa, Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayzah, and along with them some polytheist tribes who lived around Madinah.

Apparently these circumstances were temporary circumstances, practical conditions which the Muslims faced, and were not permanent international regulations of the Islamic state or Islamic system. Because later amendments were made to them, and the commands that came in Surah Bara'ah were the final commands.

Regarding the stages through which international relations passed, we had quoted from Imam Ibn al-Qayyim's book Zad al-Ma'ad in Part Nine. It is appropriate here to present that excerpt again.

Under the heading "The Prophet's conduct towards disbelievers and hypocrites from his commission until his death," he writes:

Allah, the Exalted, first revealed to him the revelation: "Read in the name of your Lord." Thus began his prophethood. At that time the command given was that he should read to himself. He had not yet been commanded to preach. After some time, this verse was revealed: "O you who are wrapped up, arise and warn." So through "Read" he received prophethood, and through "O you who are wrapped up" he was granted the office of messengership, and he was commanded to warn his relatives. After his relatives, he warned his people of an evil end. After the people, he preached to the tribes scattered around Makkah al-Mukarramah. After this, this message was spread throughout the entire Arab world, and finally this call was made an international call.

After beginning the work of the Islamic call, the Prophet ﷺ for several years only admonished and preached and did not use force. Rather, he was commanded to exercise patience and forgiveness, and not to answer a brick with a stone. After a period, he was given permission to migrate, and at the same time he was also permitted to fight the enemies, though this permission was to the extent that fighting should be waged only against those who came out onto the battlefield to fight, and not against others. Last of all, it was commanded that fighting against the disbelievers and polytheists should continue until the religion becomes entirely for Allah (li-yakūna al-dīn kulluhu lillāh). When the command for jihad was given, the relations between the Prophet and the disbelievers had only three forms: the people of peace (ahl al-sulh), the people of war (ahl al-harb), and the people of protection (ahl al-dhimmah). Regarding the people of peace, that is, those with whom peace treaties had been concluded, the command was that the covenant should be kept to the end, but only in the case that the opposing side abided by its treaty. If they committed breach of covenant and treachery, then the Prophet too should throw the treaty back in their faces, but practically no war should be launched against such people until they were formally informed that the treaty had ended. When Surah Bara'ah was revealed, all these categories of commands were explained separately. Allah, the Exalted, commanded the Prophet ﷺ to fight the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) until they either pay the jizyah or enter Islam, and jihad was also commanded against the polytheists and hypocrites. Moreover, a command was given to be more severe with the hypocrites. The Prophet's jihad against disbelievers was in the form of armed war, and against hypocrites it was through speech and argument.

The Urdu passage above is the second part of the commentary on Surah al-Anfal 8:55. It is the continuation of a discussion that began earlier in the commentary, and it contains Qur'anic verses, a hadith-related and historical discussion, and references to Ibn Qayyim.

Here is the translation:

In Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah), it was also ordered that all treaties made with the disbelievers be terminated and that disassociation from them be openly declared. After this declaration, the people of covenant were divided into three categories. The first were those against whom war was commanded. These were the people who had broken their covenant and did not remain steadfast in their agreement. The Prophet (ﷺ) fought against these people and gained victory over them. The second category was of those with whom there was a covenant and who continued to fulfill it. The Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to uphold the treaty with them for its stipulated term and to abide by its conditions. The third category consisted of people with whom there was no treaty, or who had not joined any war against the Prophet (ﷺ), or with whom a treaty had been concluded without a specified term. Regarding such people, it was ordered that they be given a respite of four months, and that they be told that no treaty would be made with them after that, [and that they must either accept Islam] or prepare to fight.

In accordance with these instructions, the Prophet (ﷺ) fought against those who had broken their covenants. He granted a respite of four months to those who had no covenant, and he fulfilled his covenant with the upright covenanters. All such people became part of the believers and the Muslims before the term of the treaty was completed, and the jizyah was imposed on the people of dhimmah.

As has been said, after the revelation of Surah Bara'ah, the Prophet's relations with the disbelievers were reduced to three types: those at war (muharibun), the people of dhimmah (ahl al-dhimmah), and the people of covenant (ahl al-'ahd). Since all of them entered Islam, only the people of dhimmah and the people at war remained. The condition of the people at war was that during his time they always feared him.

Thus, in the final period of the Prophet's (ﷺ) life, the nature of the relations between him and all people was only this: some of them were Muslims and believers, some were at peace and in amity, and some feared him and were at war with him.

Regarding the Prophet's (ﷺ) conduct with the hypocrites, Allah had commanded him to accept their outward declaration of Islam, to leave their inner state to Allah, and to use only the weapons of knowledge and reasoning against them. He was to adopt a cold attitude towards them, to be firm with them, and, keeping their psychological condition in view, to strive to reform them through his exalted teachings. He was not to take part in their funeral prayers, nor was he to stand at their graves to supplicate, and even if he asked forgiveness for them, Allah would certainly not forgive them. This was the brief account of the Prophet's (ﷺ) conduct towards his disbelieving and hypocritical enemies.

From the study of this summary, the study of the events of the biography (sirah), and the study of the occasions of revelation of these verses, it is evident that the circumstances in which Surah al-Anfal was revealed were a transitional stage between the early circumstances of Madinah and the final circumstances presented in Surah al-Tawbah. Therefore, keeping these historical stages in mind is necessary for studying these verses. Although there are some definitive principles in them, these were given in their final form in Surah al-Tawbah, and were practically implemented in the final days of the Prophet's (ﷺ) life.

In light of this detailed statement of Ibn Qayyim, we now explain the Qur'anic texts:

﴿Indeed, the most evil of creatures in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve, so they do not believe. Those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant every time, and they do not fear Allah.﴾

The word dawab, though linguistically applied to all things that move on the earth, and therefore also applies to human beings, when applied to humans, is intended to give the matter a particular colouring, namely to give humanity the colour and shade of animality. Thus the impression is given about those people to whom this word is applied that they are the worst of beasts. These are people who have adopted the way of disbelief, and whose circumstances have brought them to the point that they are no longer going to believe. For the distinguishing feature of these people is that they break covenants and do not fear Allah.

Regarding who is meant by this verse, several reports have been transmitted. Some said it refers to Banu Qurayzah. Some said it refers to Banu Nadir. Some reports state it refers to Banu Qaynuqa'. Some said it refers to the Arab tribes living around Madinah. The words of the verse and the historical events both indicate that all these groups may be meant, since each group of Jews breached the covenant with the Prophet (ﷺ) in its own place, and the polytheists around Madinah also repeatedly broke covenants. The truth is that this verse comments on all the events that occurred before and after Badr. However, the command given is for the Day of Resurrection, and it applies to all those people and all those circumstances that will occur along this pattern until the Day of Resurrection.

Those who took the path of disbelief have gone far in disbelief, and have adopted such a course that there is no longer any possibility of their believing. Thus corruption has entered their nature, and they have become the worst of beasts.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verse 56:

The attitude of these people is that whatever covenant they make, they break it. By doing so, they have been stripped of an important characteristic of humanity, namely fidelity to covenants. They have become free of every restraint in the same way that beasts (bahaim) are free, although beasts are bound within their natural law, whereas for these people there is no compelling natural law. Therefore, in the sight of Allah, they are regarded as a creation even worse than beasts.

For such people, whose covenants and pledges no one can rely upon and whose protection of neighbourhood is not secure, the appropriate recompense and punishment is that they be deprived of peace and security, just as they themselves have deprived other people of peace. Their punishment is that they be made fearful, expelled from the territory, and that their hands be broken and set aside. A blow should be struck against them such that they are not only frightened, but that this blow becomes a lesson for all those who remain behind them. This is the command given to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and in the same way, this command also applies to those who come after him. If they are confronted with such people, they should adopt this same approach.

This is a strange manner of speech. In it there is a picture of a terrifying grip and a dreadful awe and majesty. On hearing it, people become ready to flee and to abandon their positions. This will be the state of those who hear and see. As for those to whom this punishment is given, their condition is known: what will it be? This is the blow which Allah has commanded His Messenger to deliver, and along with being terrifying, it is also a lesson for those who have prepared for breaking covenants and have abandoned human rules and regulations. These instructions were given so that the Islamic front might breathe in peace, and that, because of its awe, external powers, whoever they may be, would be so struck with fear that they would not stand as obstacles in the path of the spread of Islam, whether they were near or far.

This is the temperament of the Islamic system of life, and it should settle well in the mind of the Islamic movement that this religion requires awe and dread, and it requires strength. It necessarily requires a terrifying majesty, and it is necessary that those tyrannical powers be overawed so that they do not become obstacles in the path of the spread of Islam, because Islam is the standard-bearer of human freedom across the whole earth, and it wants to deliver mankind from every tyrannical power. Those who think that the method of this religion is to rely merely on da'wah (invitation) and tabligh (propagation), and not to touch the material obstacles which tyranny has erected, are people who have not at all understood the temperament of this religion.

That was the first ruling concerning those who had actually committed a breach of covenant. Regarding them it was said that they should be dealt with in such a way, and that such a decisive blow should be struck upon them, that there would be a lesson for them and, after them, for other onlookers and listeners, and that it would instill fear into their camps.

The second ruling concerns those people from whom the signs of breach of covenant have already appeared, and from whom it is expected that they will soon commit a breach of covenant. When these signs are clear, the ruling regarding such people is: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their covenant] openly. Indeed, Allah does not like the treacherous.﴾

Islam makes a covenant so that it may be acted upon. When the second party does not intend to act upon it, then Islam announces before it the cancellation of that covenant and openly terminates it. Islam does not endorse treachery and betrayal. Islam also does not tolerate deceit and trickery. Islam openly and clearly tells the second party that it has cancelled that covenant, so that now neither party is bound by the terms of that covenant. In this way, Islam grants humanity the status of honour and steadfastness, and grants a wide sphere of peace and tranquility. Islam does not accept that one should attack, by means of a night raid and breach of promise, those people who are content in the security of a covenant and treaty and who have not been notified that the attacking party has ended the covenant. Likewise, Islam does not wish to frighten those people who have not taken precautionary measures and from whom Islam faces only the danger of treachery. However, after the covenant has been terminated, war stratagems may be employed during the battle, because war stratagems are permissible during war, since the enemy has received notice. It has taken precautionary measures. Now if a war stratagem is employed against it, it is not excused but negligent, and if a war stratagem is employed against the negligent, it is not treachery.

Islam wishes to raise the level of humanity. It wishes that humanity be free from defilements. Therefore, Islam does not consider treachery permissible for the sake of dominance, while it is striving for lofty aims, because adopting a noble manner is necessary for lofty aims.

Islam is strongly opposed to treachery, and it regards those who commit breach of covenant as extremely contemptible. Therefore, Islam does not permit its followers to commit treachery in a covenant, even if the goals and objectives for which this action is being taken are very lofty. The human self cannot be divided into pieces. Once a person begins to adopt base and vile methods, he can never adopt a lofty and noble conduct. A person who considers it permissible to use every kind of means for good objectives is not a Muslim. Therefore, this principle is entirely alien to Islamic thought and Islamic consciousness, because in the Islamic mentality there is no distinction between ends and means, since a Muslim who wishes to reach a pure and clean place will not pass through filthy mud, for their dirty feet would make even the clean place dirty. If anyone considers it permissible, he is treacherous, and Allah does not like the treacherous. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous.﴾

Here we should reflect on the circumstances in which these commands were being revealed. What was the status of humanity in those circumstances? In them, humanity did not have such a lofty ideal before it. In that era, those fighting one another followed the law of the jungle. The law of the club prevailed, and there was no restraint on the club and on plunder. From that time until the eighteenth century, this law of the jungle remained prevalent in the world, and Europe in particular was in such darkness that it did not even know of international law until that time. It obtained this light when its contact with Islamic countries increased, and to this day Europe has not reached, in international affairs, the level that the Islamic system reached in a single leap. Yet Europe had at least heard the name of international law. Those who are today overawed by Europe's industrial progress should reflect on this subject and undertake a comparative study of Islam's international law and the legal systems of the modern age, so that they may become aware of the true state of affairs.

These instructions and this clean policy lead to Allah's promise that, as a result, the Muslims will attain victory and success, and that confronting the power of the disbelievers will become very easy for them.

The secret counsels of these people and their plots to commit treachery will fail to make them successful or to give them superiority over the Muslims, because Allah stands behind the Muslims. And treacherous people cannot escape from Allah. When Allah wishes to seize the disbelievers, they cannot oppose Him. And when Allah wishes to help the Muslims, these cannot defeat them.

Therefore, those who adopt good means for good ends, if their intention is correct, should remain content that those who use base weapons cannot get ahead of them, because they have Allah's help, and they want to establish the Sunnah of Allah upon this earth; they are striving to raise the word of Allah. They walk in the name of Allah, and their aim is to bring people out of all forms of slavery and into the worship and servitude of Allah alone, with none associated with Him.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 8, verse 60:

But Islam also commands that the Muslim community, within the bounds of its strength, adopt every lawful means it can and make preparation, even though it is assured that it has the help of God. Even so, it is their duty to keep their preparation complete and to provide the means that human nature recognises and that lie within human experience. Islam advises these people to look toward the help of the higher realm only when they have made complete outward preparation and are ready for realistic struggle, so that the lofty goals that Islam has in view may be achieved.

Preparing according to one's power and capacity is necessary alongside the obligation of jihad. This verse commands Muslims to keep various kinds of military preparations and equipment ready, and here the horses kept ready for battle are mentioned in particular, because they were an important part of the military equipment of the time when the Qur'an was being revealed. Had the Qur'an at that time commanded the preparation of the equipment of the present age instead of horses, it would have been an unknown and astonishing equipment, and people would have been amazed merely on hearing of it. Therefore God spoke in accordance with people's level of understanding, and it cannot be expected of God that He would say something that its addressees could not even comprehend. The fitting course is to issue a general command, and it is this: "Wa-a'iddu lahum ma istatatum min quwwah" ("And prepare against them whatever you can of strength"). Islam requires that it possess the necessary strength, and that it advance on the basis of that strength and liberate all people from every kind of slavery. Accordingly, the first duty of this strength is to free people to such an extent that they are free to accept any ideology they choose. No one should stand in their way, and there should be no power in the world capable of compelling anyone to adopt any particular belief. The second duty is that this strength should so terrify the enemies of the religion of Islam that they cannot even think of attacking the centre of the Islamic power, the Dar al-Islam. And the third duty is that the enemies of the religion of Islam should be so overawed that they do not think, at any time, of blocking the path of Islam, so that the Islamic movement may be able to liberate all human beings who dwell on this earth. And the fourth duty is that this very Islamic strength should shatter to pieces all the powers that establish their sovereignty in opposition to God and that impose their own sovereignty and their own law upon people in opposition to God, and that do not acknowledge that sovereignty belongs solely to God, for He alone is the Deity, without partner.

Islam is not a monastic system confined to beliefs and ideas, or one that is concerned only with certain acts of worship and whose function ends there. Rather, Islam is a practical system for the whole of life, and it stands up against all other systems and wages war against all the powers that stand behind those false systems. Therefore, Islam has no other path but to shatter to pieces all the powers that stand in its way, because these powers block the path of Islam and do not let it be established, and, on the contrary, these powers establish other systems in opposition to Islam.

At the proclamation of this great truth, no Muslim should mumble or speak hastily and offhandedly so that no one can understand. Nor should Muslims feel shame in proclaiming this truth; rather, they should proclaim it with their heads held high and say that this is in fact a movement for human freedom, and that it is its standard-bearer. It is not the standard-bearer of any human system of life, nor does it seek the establishment of the rule of any leader, nor does it seek the rule of any class, race, group or sect. Its aim is not to enslave the peasants so that they serve the landowners, as was the aim of the Roman civilisation; nor is its aim to conquer the world and seize all the raw materials of the world in order to feed its industries, as was the aim of Western imperialism; nor has it arisen to establish the dictatorship of some party in a region and reduce other people to slaves like cattle, as was the case in the communist system. Rather, it is the standard-bearer for the establishment of the sovereignty of the All-Knowing and All-Wise, the All-Hearing and All-Seeing. It seeks the establishment of God's sovereignty and seeks to deliver all human beings in the world from every kind of slavery, such that no servant is a slave to another servant.

This is the great truth which Muslims whose mentality has been defeated should well understand, those who unduly defend the religion of Islam and the Islamic system and who, even in that defence, merely mumble and cannot state anything clearly and plainly, and who search for lame excuses for the Islamic doctrine of jihad. (For details, see the valuable treatise "Al-Jihad fi'l-Islam" by Abu'l-A'la Mawdudi, Amir of the Jamaat-e-Islami Pakistan.) Likewise, it is also essential to study the detailed discussion we have presented on the Islamic doctrine of jihad in the introduction to Surat al-Anfal.

Furthermore, in this verse we must also thoroughly know the limits of the preparation that we have been commanded to make: "wa-a'iddu lahum ma istatatum", that is, to the extent that you are able, meaning that you should expend your full strength in preparation, that is, all the means of war and victory should be provided, that is, to the fullest possible extent.

Then, the purpose of the preparation has also been stated in this verse: "turhibuna bihi 'aduwwa Allahi wa-'aduwwakum wa-akharina min dunihim la ta'lamunahum Allahu ya'lamuhum" ("so that by it you may strike terror into the enemy of God and your enemy, and others besides them whom you do not know but whom God knows").

That is, so that by it you may be able to frighten your enemies and the enemies of God, and those other enemies whom you do not know but God knows. That is, the aims of this preparation are that your enemies, who are the enemies of God, be terrified. Among them are the open enemies whom the Muslims know, and some enemy powers stand behind them, whose existence is not known to the Muslims but is known to God, because they have not declared their enmity, and God knows the secrets of their hearts. The power of Islam will overawe these people, even though the military strength of the Muslims may not yet have reached them in practice. In short, it is an obligation upon Muslims that they be people of strength, and it is also an obligation upon them that they gather strength to the extent of their capacity, so that they are a source of fear to all the people of the earth, and this is so that the word of God may be exalted in the world and the religion may belong entirely to God.

Now, since military preparations will involve expenses, and since at that time Islamic society was functioning solely on the basis of mutual solidarity, therefore, along with the command for military preparation, it was commanded: spend your wealth in the way of God. "Wa-ma tunfiqu min shay'in fi sabili Allahi yuwaffa ilaykum wa-antum la tuzlamun" ("And whatever you spend in the way of God will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be wronged"). In this way Islam purifies jihad in the way of God and spending in the way of God from all worldly aims and purposes. It elevates these aims above personal desires and detaches them from every kind of national, class and territorial consciousness and passion, so that they may be purely for the sake of God and for the pleasure of God.

This is why Islam, from its very beginning, prohibits all wars that are fought for the supremacy of certain individuals, or fought for the supremacy of certain governments, or fought for the seizure of markets, or fought to dominate and humiliate people; or fought for the supremacy of one country over another, or fought for the supremacy of one nation over another, or fought for the supremacy of one race or for the supremacy of one class over other classes. Islam permits only one kind of war, namely jihad in the way of God. And God does not wish that one race should dominate other races, or one homeland and other homelands, or one class over other classes, or one individual over other individuals, or one nation over other nations, so as to establish its own sovereignty, its own government and its own supreme authority. He is free of need of all the worlds. He wishes only that His sovereignty be established in the world, so that goodness and blessing, freedom and nobility may prevail in the world. And this can be achieved only under the shelter of the sovereignty of God.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verse 61 (part 1 of 2):

The third ruling in these verses concerns those peoples who wish to enter into a covenant of friendship and peace with the Islamic camp, who incline towards peace and security, and whose outward circumstances also confirm that these people genuinely desire peace.

﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it too, and put your trust in Allah. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

This is a subtle expression. That is, the bird inclines towards peace and conciliation, and the bird is softening its wings, and a state of peace, reconciliation and amity is expressed. Then, in reconciliation and truce, the command to rely upon Allah has also been given. He who is Sami' (All-Hearing) and 'Alim (All-Knowing) hears every word and can see hidden intentions, and reliance upon Allah is a very great guarantor.

Now let us return to the summary that Imam Ibn al-Qayyim presented concerning the external relations of the Islamic state: what the Prophet's relations with the disbelievers were in the early period of Madinah, that is, up to the Battle of Badr and the revelation of these commands. This summary shows that this group belongs to the category of those with whom the Prophet ﷺ adopted a policy of peace and did not wage jihad or fighting. This is because these people were inclined towards peace with the Prophet and had not shown hostility. Nor had they stood in the way of the call of Islam. They did not take any action against the Islamic state. Allah had commanded the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to leave these people in their condition and to accept their offer of reconciliation and peace (this command remained in force until Surah Bara'ah (Surah al-Tawbah) was revealed, and those with whom there was no formal covenant were given a fixed period of grace, or those with whom there was a covenant without a specified time were given a period of four months, and at its conclusion relations were again reset). Therefore, the above-mentioned command was not the final and last command; it was a specific ruling for particular circumstances, and later commands abrogated it, and the Prophet ﷺ himself also made changes to it.

Yes, this verse was a general ruling in its own time, and until the revelation of Surah Bara'ah this was the ruling in practice. The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, which took place in the sixth century Hijri, was also an example of this.

Some jurists hold that this ruling is final and conclusive, and they have explained the meaning of inclining to peace (junahu lil-silm) as meaning that they accept paying the jizya (poll tax on non-Muslim subjects). But this opinion is contrary to historical events. This is because the rulings on jizya were revealed in Surah Bara'ah, and this surah was revealed in the eighth year of the Hijri calendar, while the verse under commentary was revealed after the Battle of Badr in the second year of the Hijri calendar. At that time the rulings on jizya did not exist. If one considers the revolutionary character of the Islamic system of life, the circumstances of the revelation of the Qur'an and the events of the Seerah (Prophetic biography), it appears most probable that this ruling is not final. It has been modified and amended by the rulings revealed in Surah Bara'ah, in which the relations of Muslims with other peoples have been regulated in such a way that they are either people of war, who will be in active war against the Muslims; or they will be Muslims, who will implement the Shariah of Allah; or they will be ahl al-dhimmah (protected non-Muslim subjects) who pay the jizya. And they will remain ahl al-dhimmah for as long as they remain faithful to the covenant of their protected status. This is the final form of international relations to which the Islamic movement of jihad ultimately leads. Beyond this, if any other situation exists, it is in fact a practical situation which exists in practice, but the Islamic system strives to change it, and this striving continues until the three situations mentioned above are established, which were mentioned in Surah Bara'ah and which are the final rulings. These final rulings are present in the narration of Muslim, which Imam Ahmad has narrated.

Ahmad narrates from Waki', from Sufyan, from Alqamah ibn Martad, from Sulayman ibn Buraydah, from his father, from Yazid ibn al-Khatib al-Aslami, who says: When the Prophet ﷺ would send someone as a commander of an army or as a leader of a detachment, he would advise him to fear Allah and to be sincerely good to the Muslims with him. He then said: "Fight in the name of Allah, in the path of Allah. Fight those who disbelieve in Allah. And when you meet your enemies among the polytheists, invite them to choose one of three positions. Whichever of them they accept, you should accept it from them, and leave them in their condition. Invite them to Islam; if they become Muslims, accept it from them. Then invite them to migrate from their land to the land of the Muhajirin (emigrants). If they accept this position, then their rights and those of the Muhajirin will be equal, and they will have the same obligations as the Muhajirin. If they refuse and prefer to remain in their own land, inform them that their status will be like that of the Muslims who are Bedouin (a'rab). The commands of Allah will apply to them, just as they apply to the Bedouin Muslims, but they will have no share in fai' (revenue from non-combat sources) and ghanimah (spoils of war), unless they participate in jihad with the Muslims. If they refuse even this position, then offer them that they pay the jizya. If they accept, then you also accept it and refrain from fighting. And if they refuse, then seek the help of Allah and begin fighting."

The difficulty in this narration is that it mentions emigration (hijrah) and the abode of the emigrants, and then also mentions jizya. Yet jizya was made obligatory after the Conquest of Makkah, and after the Conquest of Makkah the emigration had ended. (That is, when the first community of Muslims came to Madinah and attained stability until the conquest, the emigration had then ended.) And it is established from the ahadith and history that jizya was made obligatory in the eighth year of the Hijrah. This is why no Arab polytheist was ever taken jizya from, because all the Arabs had become Muslims before the obligation of jizya. After this year, jizya was taken from the Magians and from polytheists. And if there had been any polytheists among the Arabs at the time jizya was made obligatory, they would certainly also have paid jizya, as Imam Ibn al-Qayyim explained. The opinion of Imam Abu Hanifah, and according to one view of Imam Ahmad, is also this. (Qurtubi has also reported this view from Imam al-Awza'i and Malik.)

In any case, there is no mention of a final ruling in the verse under discussion, "wa in junahu" (and if they incline). The final rulings of this series were revealed later in Surah Bara'ah. In it, Allah commanded the Messenger of Allah to accept the offer of peace and reconciliation from those whom he had left in their condition and with whom he had not begun fighting, whether or not there had been a covenant with them until then. So he continued to accept the reconciliation of disbelievers and People of the Book up to the time of Surah Bara'ah, and after the revelation of Bara'ah the command became that you must either accept Islam or pay jizya. This state of reconciliation is acceptable only as long as people remain faithful to their covenant; otherwise the Muslims will fight against them as long as they are able, so that the religion becomes entirely for Allah.

I have been somewhat lengthy in the explanation and commentary of this verse, so that the doubts of those people who are intellectually defeated may be removed. When such people sit down to write on the subject of the Islamic doctrine of jihad, they come under the pressure of present circumstances, and their thinking and their spirit sit down under the weight of these circumstances. They cannot even believe that it could be a permanent principle of the religion of Islam that you either accept Islam or pay jizya, otherwise prepare for war. When these people see that at this time all the forces of jahiliyyah (ignorance) and taghut (tyranny) are fighting against Islam and confronting it, and that the people of Islam call themselves Muslims but are unaware of the reality of Islam, and do not have a true consciousness of Islam in their hearts and minds, and feel themselves to be very weak before the great powers of other religions, then on the other hand they see that the vanguards of Islam are very few and rare, and are also weak and frail. Therefore, in these circumstances, those who write distort the Qur'an and Sunnah and make interpretations of them, and they do this solely under the pressure of circumstances. So they adopt a position which Islam cannot bear, nor can it be derived from the texts of Islam.

These people argue from those verses which were revealed as temporary guidance for the Islamic movement. They regard those verses as final instructions and interpret the final instructions accordingly. Yet the verses from which they argue were temporary and relevant texts. Why do they do this? So that they may prove that the Islamic doctrine of jihad has only the purpose of defending the Dar al-Islam and the Muslim community, that jihad can begin only when the enemy attacks, and that Islam accepts every kind of offer of peace and security. And in their view, peace and security means only that someone agrees to refrain from attacking the Dar al-Islam. According to the concept of these people, Islam may do whatever it wishes within its own borders, but it has no right to demand that others accept Islam. Nor does it have the right to demand that people obey the Islamic system. Islam has only the right of preaching. As for that power, the tyrannical power, which stands behind jahiliyyah, Islam has no right to challenge that power, or, if that power challenges Islam, Islam has only the right of defence.

If such people, who have been defeated intellectually and spiritually by present circumstances, were to think carefully and seek in the Qur'an and Sunnah rulings that correspond to present circumstances, and did not take the path of interpretations in which the texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah are twisted and presented, then they would find in the texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah texts concerning situations similar to their present circumstances. This is because Islam has been a realistic and dynamic religion, and they could say that in such circumstances Islam had decided thus, and we too should do likewise. Then these gentlemen would not have had any need to make such interpretations of the final instructions and texts of the Qur'an. They could say that these rulings of Islam are appropriate in the present circumstances, but they are not final rulings. They are temporary measures.

Islam did in fact adopt different strategies in different circumstances. Consider a few examples, and these examples were according to the temporary need.

When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah, he concluded a covenant with the Jews and the polytheists living around Madinah, in which matters of mutual brotherhood, peace and joint defence were settled. It was also agreed that the sovereignty of Madinah would belong to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that in defence against the Quraysh all these people would stand with the Muslims. And that whoever attacked Madinah, these people would have no relationship with that attacker. They would not make any covenant with the polytheists unless the Prophet ﷺ permitted it. Meanwhile, Allah had commanded the Prophet that whichever people made a covenant of peace and security, their offer should be accepted, even if they did not make a formal written agreement; in any case, as long as they wished for peace, peace would be maintained. After this, all these rulings were changed, as we have explained in detail above.

Similarly, when the enemies of the Prophet all combined against him at the time of the Battle of the Trench, the Banu Qurayzah also broke their promise, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sensed the danger that the Muslims might be wiped out entirely. So the Prophet offered reconciliation to 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari and al-Harith ibn 'Awf al-Murri, chief of Ghatafan, and agreed that they would be given one third of the produce of Madinah, and that they would take their peoples and return, leaving the Quraysh alone. The Prophet's offer was intended to win their favour; it was not a covenant. When the Prophet saw that these two men had become willing, he consulted Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah. Both said: "O Messenger of Allah, if you like this matter, we will accept it for your sake; and if it is a command of Allah, we will obey; or if you are doing this for us..." The Prophet said: "I wish to take this step to protect you, because all the Arabs are shooting arrows at you from one bow." Upon this, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, we were in shirk, we were idol-worshippers, we did not worship Allah and we had no knowledge of Allah. These polytheists did not expect of us that we would give them even a single date, unless they bought it, or we gave it to them as hospitality. And when Allah honoured us through Islam, and gave us guidance through the Qur'an, and through you we became honourable, shall we now give them our wealth? We will give them the sword, so that it may decide between us and them." The Prophet was very pleased with this answer, and said: "(You know best, and they)," and said to 'Uyaynah and al-Harith: "Come, we have nothing for you but the sword." This matter, about which the Prophet thought in particular circumstances, was a temporary strategy for a need within specific circumstances; it was not a final ruling.

An example of this is the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, concluded by the Messenger (ﷺ) with the Quraysh on the occasion of Hudaybiyyah. These people were polytheists, and some of the terms of that agreement were such that the Muslims were not pleased with them. For instance, there would be no fighting between the Muslims and the Quraysh for ten years; people would live in peace with one another; the Muslims would return without performing 'Umrah that year and would come to Makkah the following year; and they (the Quraysh) allowed the Muslims to enter Makkah the following year for only three days, and they would bring only the weapons that a rider carries, and even these would be sheathed. And that if any Muslim went from Madinah to Makkah, he would have to be returned, but if anyone went from Makkah to Madinah, the polytheists would not be bound to return him. The Messenger (ﷺ) agreed to this treaty because Allah had informed him, through inspiration (ilham), that these conditions, although they apparently seemed to favour the Quraysh, were in reality beneficial for the Muslims. In this example too there is room to see that the leadership of Islam can make particular decisions in particular circumstances.

Islam is a perpetual movement, and its conduct too is movement-oriented. It makes decisions according to circumstances. It possesses a leadership that is extremely clear, firm and tested. Whatever circumstances people may face, they are in every case given guidance suited to those circumstances from the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and they never have any need to resort to far-fetched interpretation (ta'wil). What is desired in Islam is that a person should have taqwa (God-consciousness) and should be careful not to hand over his religion to the wicked leadership of jahiliyyah (ignorance); he should not be defeated, nor adopt an apologetic, defensive stance in the face of jahiliyyah, whereas the religion of Islam is dominant, the one that overcomes. It meets all the needs and problems of humanity, and it has the disposition to rise high, and to hold the initiative in every affair and in the resolution of every problem.

When Allah commanded the Messenger (ﷺ) that if anyone wished to make friendship he should accept that friendship, and if anyone inclined towards peace and security, he too should incline towards it, at the same time He also commanded him to rely upon Allah, and reassured him that if those who make such agreements have deceit in their hearts, then nothing of theirs is in any case hidden from Allah.

﴿And if they incline towards peace, then incline towards it too, and put your trust in Allah. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verses 62–63:**

Now Allah reassures and protects His Messenger from the deceit of these people. If they intend treachery and plot, and if there is a scheme of betrayal behind the peace and friendship, then He says: be content, Allah is sufficient, He is the Protector, He is the Helper, and in Badr His help was with you. Through the believers He supported you. He gave unity and harmony to the believers, although in the age of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) unity and harmony among them was not possible at all. This is the achievement of Allah, the All-Wise and All-Powerful.

﴿Allah is sufficient for you.﴾ It was He who helped you at the beginning of the movement, and He gave you a truly sincere group of believers who fulfilled the covenant they had made with Allah in full. He gave them the form of a united force, although before this their hearts were in pieces. Their mutual enmity was open, and their mutual fighting was of the most severe kind. Here what is meant may be the Aws and Khazraj, who were the Ansar, and in the age of jahiliyyah there was an endless chain of revenge upon revenge between them, and reconciliation between them was not even possible, let alone that such brotherhood should arise between them as has no parallel in the history of the whole world. Or what is meant may be the Muhajirun, who were in Makkah in the same circumstances in which the Ansar were. Or what is meant may be all the Arabs, because before Islam the condition of all the Arabs in the Arabian Peninsula was just like that.

In any case, this miracle took place on the land of the Arabs, and in reality no power and no means except Allah could have brought about this miracle. And this task could be accomplished only through the Islamic worldview (nazariyah-i-hayat). So these hearts that had hatred for one another, and these people who could not bear each other's temperament, became a single body in which immense brotherly love arose, their hearts were joined to one another, they became gentle towards one another, became intimate companions (yar-i-ghar), and their brotherhood, friendship, unity and harmony became a historical example. The predominant colour of their collective life was the colour of love, and they were a prelude and an example for the life of struggle.

﴿And We shall remove whatever rancour is in their breasts; they will be brothers, facing one another on couches.﴾ And the rancour that was in their hearts, We will remove it; they will become brothers and sit on couches facing one another.

The Islamic worldview is a strange and practical belief. When it mixes into the hearts, it appears in the form of a temperament whose colour is affection and love. Its bearers become close friends. They become a carpet for their companions; their sides become soft, and harshness is removed from their dealings and conduct. Deep connections and relationships come into being among them. Circumstances arise in which a single glance of the eye, a slight touch of the hand, words spoken, the beating of hearts, mutual affection, friendship, sympathy, self-sacrifice and sacrifice come about, the reality of which only that Being knows who created these circumstances. And the taste of their reality only the person in whom this revolution has taken place can savour.

This belief gives humanity the lifeblood of love for the sake of Allah (al-hubb fi'llah). It gives the strings of humanity the melody of sincerity, love and union, and when humanity accepts this worldview, this miracle comes to pass. And it is Allah alone who brings this miracle into being.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Among the servants of Allah there are some servants who are neither prophets nor martyrs, but on the Day of Resurrection the prophets and martyrs will long for their rank and station." The Companions said: "Will you tell us who these people are?" He said: "They are the people who love one another for the sake of the spiritual values of Allah, although there is no kinship between them and no worldly interest exists between them. By Allah, their faces are light and they are upon light. They will not be in fear when all people are in fear, and they will not be distressed when all people are distressed." (Abu Dawud)

And in another hadith the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When a Muslim meets his Muslim brother and takes his hand in his hand, the sins of both fall away just as dry leaves fall from trees on a day of strong wind, and Allah forgives the sins of both of them, even if they are as numerous as the foam of the seas." (Tabarani)

Regarding this subject, the sayings of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ are extremely numerous. And in the mission of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, all these sayings are a witness of justice to the importance of mutual love and affection. Moreover, from the formation and development of the Muslim ummah it is also evident that these sayings were not mere slogans, nor were they pleasing words. They were not merely individual actions or rare examples, but rather a reality that was manifest in the form of the Muslim ummah and the Islamic society. By the permission of Allah it rose high, and it was a minaret that no one but Allah could have erected.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verses 64–65:

Commentary on verses 64 to 65: Now the Messenger (ﷺ) is given reassurance, and through him the Muslim community is reassured, that Allah is your friend and protector, and you are His friends. You are sufficient, and He is sufficient for you. Therefore, be eager to fight in the way of Allah, and because of the power of faith within you, one of you possesses the strength of ten. And even if the believers become very weak, they will still defeat enemies twice their number.

Here human thinking stands still. It reflects upon this unconquerable strength and is left astonished. This strength is the strength of Allah, who is most powerful and dominant. Set against the strength of Allah is the insignificant human strength that challenges the armies of Allah. Between the two there is the difference of heaven and earth. This struggle has a certainly protected outcome, its result is clear, and the guarantee of Allah stands behind it. The guarantee of Allah is:

﴿O Prophet, sufficient for you is Allah and for those who follow you of the believers.﴾ That is: O Prophet, for you and for the believers who follow you, Allah alone is sufficient. For this reason, after this, the believers are told to become eager for fighting in the way of Allah. This command is given in circumstances in which every person is ready for it, every heart is prepared, the nerves of all the believers are tensed for it, the veins and fibres are inclined toward it, and the vessel of the heart is filled with faith, tranquility and trust in Allah.

﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight. If there are twenty among you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a hundred among you, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve, because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ O Prophet, urge the believers to fight and prepare them, because they are equal to the enemies of Allah and their own enemies. Although they are few in number and the enemy is more numerous and spread around them.

﴿If there are among you twenty who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a hundred, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve.﴾ If twenty of you are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred, and if there are a hundred, they will prevail over a thousand of the disbelievers. Why is this so? This matter is very sudden and strange, yet it has depth and truth within it.

﴿Because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ At first sight there seems to be no connection between understanding (fiqh) and victory in war. But between them there is a real and very strong connection. The believing forces know well what their path is, what their method is, what the reality of that Being is, and what their purpose of existence is. Indeed, the company of believers knows well what the station of divinity is and what the etiquettes of servitude are. They know that divinity is unique and exalted, and that the etiquette of servitude is that worship is offered to Allah alone, with no partner with Him. The company of believers also knows this: they are the Muslim community, they are the bearers of Allah's guidance, and this company has been raised up in the world for this reason, that people be brought out of the servitude and slavery of other people and enter into the worship of Allah alone. Only the one who is Allah's vicegerent is that one; he has not been placed upon this earth so that he may exalt himself and live in luxury, but so that he may exalt the word of Allah, strive in His way, fill this earth with truth, judge among people with justice, and establish upon this earth a dominion whose purpose is to establish justice among people. This is the understanding (fiqh) which fills the hearts of the believers with light, certainty and strength, and prepares them for jihad in the way of Allah, and they rise up with great strength and certainty. They have prior certainty about their end, whereas their enemies are people who do not understand these aims and objectives. Locks are upon their hearts and minds, their sight is weak, their powers are numb, even though outwardly they may appear strong and robust. Their strength is in truth cut off from its true source.

This ratio, that one man will be equal to ten men, is the real and genuine ratio, in the scale of Allah, between believers who understand and disbelievers who do not understand. But if the Muslims become very weak and feeble, the ratio of two to one will still remain between them and the disbelievers.

Here Allah wants to tell the believers: assess your strength well, do not consider yourselves to be less, and be assured. And plant your feet firmly on the field of battle. This comparison is not a legal comparison but a psychological comparison.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 8, verses 67–69:

After exhorting to fighting and stirring up zeal for it, the discourse now turns to the rulings concerning prisoners. Here, this relates to the actions of the Messenger of Allah and the Muslims at Badr. It is said: train the prisoners you hold in your custody mentally in this way; invite them to faith, and tell them that if they now believe, the opportunities they have lost before can be made up for.

Ibn Ishaq, while narrating the events of the Battle of Badr, said: "When the people began to take the enemy captive, the Messenger of Allah was in his canopy (chabutra), and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was standing guard at its door. With him were other Ansar as well, and Sa'd had his sword drawn. All these people were appointed to protect the Messenger of Allah; they feared that some attacker from the enemy might strike the Prophet. I was told that the Messenger of Allah perceived some signs of displeasure on Sa'd's face, because he did not like what the people were doing. So the Messenger of Allah said: 'Sa'd! Perhaps you do not like what these people are doing.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, your word is correct.' This was the first occasion on which Allah inflicted such a defeat on the polytheists. In my view, in that battle, annihilating the people was more appropriate than taking them alive as captives."

Imam Ahmad narrated with his chain from Ibn Abbas, who said, citing Umar: when the armies met that day, Allah inflicted defeat on the polytheists. Seventy of them were killed and seventy were taken captive. The Messenger of Allah consulted Abu Bakr, Umar and Ali (may Allah be pleased with them). Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah, these people are cousins, our own kin and brothers. My view is that you accept ransom from them, so that what we take from them will be a source of strength against the disbelievers, and it is possible that they may be guided and become a support for us." Then the Messenger of Allah said: "Ibn al-Khattab, what do you say?" He said: "I gave this advice at that occasion; by Allah, my opinion is not in accordance with the opinion of Abu Bakr. I say that you should hand over so-and-so (their relative) to me, so that I may strike off his neck; hand over Aqil ibn Abi Talib to Ali so that he may strike off his neck; and hand over his brother to Hamza so that he may strike off his neck; so that Allah may know that there is no soft corner in our hearts for the polytheists. These are their leaders and chiefs." So the Messenger of Allah adopted the opinion of Abu Bakr, did not accept my view, and accepted ransom from the people. On the next day, I went early in the morning to the Messenger of Allah and found that Abu Bakr and the Messenger were weeping. I asked: "O Messenger of Allah, what makes you and your companion weep?
